# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1761, as Massachusetts's westernmost county. Berkshire County was established by the Massachusetts General Court and has been stable ever since — it did not subdivide further during the target period.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsfield (also the site of the Probate Court and Registry of Deeds)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts (Commonwealth)
- **Population during period:** The population tool returned no data for this county for this period; 1820–1850 Massachusetts census figures at the state level document strong growth, but a specific Berkshire County figure from the tool is unavailable. The 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 federal censuses each enumerate Berkshire County fully and are searchable.
- **Economy:** Hill farming, iron manufacture, paper mills, marble quarrying, and early textile mills (particularly in Pittsfield and Adams). The Housatonic River valley drove water-powered industry.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Yankee (English-descent New England families) in this period, with some Irish immigration beginning by the 1840s following the famine. Long-standing communities of free Black residents in some towns.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant in most towns), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, and Quaker congregations. Dutch Reformed communities exist near the New York border.
- **Key historical events:** The Erie Canal (1825) drew some migration westward out of the region; the Western Railroad reached Pittsfield in 1841, transforming the county's economic ties eastward and westward simultaneously.

## Boundary changes

Berkshire County was formed in 1761 and the FamilySearch place record shows it has been a county from that date forward (`dateRange: +1761/`). No subdivision occurred during 1820–1850. The county seat and administrative geography were stable across the entire target period. Records created before 1761 for the same territory would be in the predecessor Hampshire County.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Level and start date:** In Massachusetts, vital registration was mandated at the **town level** from 1639, though compliance was uneven. Massachusetts became the first state to institute a permanent **statewide** registration system beginning in **1841** — per the `Massachusetts_Vital_Records` wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records).
- **What this means for 1820–1850:** For 1820–1840, you are dependent entirely on **town-level** records kept by individual town clerks. From 1841, state-level registrations were filed in addition to the town copy, giving you two potential sources. Marriage intentions were commonly recorded in the bride's home town; additional copies may appear in the groom's home town.
- **Published transcription series:** The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series covers over 200 Massachusetts towns and is the most accessible starting point. These are widely digitized.
- **Key FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection ID 2061550, ~3.4 million records, ~1.7 million images) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 — this is an indexed collection searchable by name.
- **Where originals are held:** The original vital records remain with the clerk of the town or city in which the event occurred, per the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page.
- **Gaps:** Coverage compliance was uneven before 1841. Not every birth or death was recorded at the town level, especially in rural areas. The state system (post-1841) improves coverage but is still not complete.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist, Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker, and Dutch Reformed (near the New York line).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Church records in this period often recorded events that town clerks missed, and in some Berkshire towns are the only surviving evidence for a birth or death.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection ID 1921657, ~987,000 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657.
- **Digitized but browse-only volume:** FamilySearch volume 004500892 covers Pittsfield Congregational Church records 1791–1850 (274 images). `recordSearchablePercent: 0`, `fulltextSearchable: false` — this volume must be browsed image-by-image. There is no name index for it.
- **Where held:** Originals are typically at the local church or the relevant diocesan or denominational archive. The FamilySearch Catalog and NEHGS (see below) hold microfilm copies of many Berkshire County church registers.
- **Language:** English throughout this period for Berkshire County.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 all enumerate Berkshire County. The 1850 census is the first to name every household member by name (earlier censuses name only the head of household). The 1850 Mortality Schedule (listing deaths in the year preceding the census) is also available and names individuals who died — a valuable supplement for death records before statewide registration was complete.
- **State census:** Massachusetts did not conduct a statewide population census to supplement federal years during this period.
- **Access:** All four federal censuses for Berkshire County are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations (intestate estates), guardianship files, inventories, and estate distributions.
- **Date range:** Berkshire County Probate Court dates from 1761.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection ID 1678901, ~567,000 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 — covers Berkshire County probate within the statewide collection.
- **Where originals are held:** Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield. Also accessible through the Massachusetts State Archives.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is a state-land state — land was granted by the colony/Commonwealth, not the federal government).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, and grantor/grantee indexes. Tax records (at the town level) also document land ownership.
- **Date range:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds records begin with county formation in 1761.
- **Where held:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield. The FamilySearch Catalog (search "Berkshire County" in the catalog) holds microfilm of deed books.
- **Note:** The wiki_search result confirms land records (deeds) were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and "survive in remarkably complete runs" statewide (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (service records for men born ca. 1770–1795); Mexican-American War (1846–1848, less directly relevant for Berkshire men).
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; War of 1812 pension files; bounty land warrants. Massachusetts state adjutant general records for militia service.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, DC, and federal repositories); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has indexed War of 1812 and earlier military records online.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Every town in Berkshire County has at least one town cemetery; denominational (Congregational, Methodist, Episcopal) burying grounds are common. Pittsfield's Pittsfield Cemetery is the county's largest secular ground of this era.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial indexing of Berkshire County cemeteries, though coverage is volunteer-dependent and incomplete. BillionGraves is a secondary source.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records (where they survive) are held by the individual town or church. The Berkshire County Historical Society holds transcriptions for some cemeteries.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Berkshire County Eagle (and its predecessors) published in Pittsfield from the early 19th century. Marriage notices, death notices, and legal notices appeared regularly.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has some historical Massachusetts newspaper coverage. The Berkshire Athenaeum (Pittsfield Public Library's local history division) holds physical and microfilm runs of county newspapers.
- **Content value:** For 1820–1850, newspapers are particularly valuable for deaths and marriages of prominent families that did not make it into town records.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Note for this place and period:** Berkshire County is inland, 140+ miles from Boston Harbor. Arrivals most relevant to this county in 1820–1850 would have entered through Boston or New York City ports.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection ID 1784312, ~1.2 million records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312 — covers Boston arrivals, indexed by name.
- **Naturalization records:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (collection ID 1459213, ~345,000 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213. Declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization were filed in any court of record, including Berkshire County courts.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — all family members are listed.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Town-level property (real estate) and personal property tax lists. Poll tax records also exist.
- **Date range:** Town tax records predate the county and run continuously through this period.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerks and/or the Massachusetts State Archives. Some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. Tax lists are especially useful as a substitute for the pre-1850 census years when only heads of household are named.

- **Town meeting records:** Every Massachusetts town kept meeting records that name residents voting, paying fines, being warned out (as non-residents), or receiving poor relief. These are held by the individual town clerk.
- **Overseers of the Poor records:** Towns maintained poor relief lists naming indigent residents — a source for people who appear nowhere else.
- **Town and county histories:** Berkshire County has a rich published local history tradition. The 19th-century "History of Berkshire County" volumes reprint early records and carry biographical sketches.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811, carved from Berks and Northampton Counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated absolutely; the county was the heart of Pennsylvania's anthracite region
- **Ethnic composition:** Welsh and English miners (est. 1840s), Irish post-Famine (post-1847), Germans, and later Slavic/Polish immigrants
- **Key events:** Schuylkill Canal → Reading Railroad dominance; the Molly Maguires trials (1875–1877); Civil War (48th Pennsylvania Infantry)

## Boundary changes

Schuylkill County's boundaries were **stable** throughout 1840–1880. Pre-1811 records fall under Berks County (south) and Northampton County (north).

---

## Key record types

### Vital records
Civil statewide registration did not begin until after 1880. **Church registers are the primary vital record source for the entire 1840–1880 window.** One marriage volume exists on FamilySearch (images 1870–1910, browse-only).

### Census records
Federal censuses for 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 all cover the county. **Note:** The 1870 census has known indexing errors — browse original images when name searches fail. Mortality schedules also exist for 1850–1880.

### Church records
One digitized FamilySearch volume (187 images, 1842–1895, English and German, **browse-only**). German-language entries require German reading ability. Welsh-congregation registers may be in Welsh.

### Probate & court records
FamilySearch volume covering 1851–1930 (412 images, **browse-only**). Also the broader Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (3.2M images, no name index). Molly Maguires trial records (1875–1877) are a unique resource naming hundreds of Irish immigrant miners.

### Land records
Deed records volume (543 images, 1815–1900) — **the only partially name-indexed volume** (22%). Pennsylvania is a state-land (metes and bounds) state; warrants and patents are at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Naturalization records
FamilySearch volume covering 1849–1915 (298 images, **browse-only**). Pre-1906 declarations could also be filed in any court of record — check NARA Philadelphia for federal court filings.

### Military records
Civil War service records and pension files indexed on Fold3/Ancestry. The 48th Pennsylvania Infantry was raised largely from Schuylkill County miners.

### Tax assessment lists (physical only)
Annual lists are the **best intercensal substitute** between census years — track adult male property holders year by year.

### Newspapers (physical/microfilm only)
Miners' Journal (Pottsville, est. 1825) ran continuously through the entire period. Obituaries, marriage notices, estate settlements, and extensive Molly Maguires trial coverage.

---

## FamilySearch digitized volumes (complete list)

| Volume | Images | Date range | Index |
|--------|--------|------------|-------|
| Probate (007936749) | 412 | 1851–1930 | Browse-only |
| Naturalization (007936750) | 298 | 1849–1915 | Browse-only |
| Church records (007936751) | 187 | 1842–1895 | Browse-only |
| Deed records (007936752) | 543 | 1815–1900 | 22% indexed |
| Marriage records (007936753) | 94 | 1870–1910 | Browse-only |

---

## Physical repositories

| Repository | Key holdings |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, probate/wills, court records, marriage records, naturalizations |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land warrants/patents, state military records, post-1893 vital records |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Miners' Journal microfilm, local histories, cemetery surveys |
| NARA Philadelphia | Federal census originals, Civil War records |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Coal company records, immigration materials |

---

## Research tips

1. **Church registers first** — civil registration hadn't started yet for 1840–1880.
2. **Deed records are the best online entry point** — the only partially indexed volume.
3. **Tax assessment lists** bridge the gap between decennial censuses (physical only).
4. **Molly Maguires trial records** are a unique finding aid for Irish miners, 1860s–1877.
5. **1870 census** — known indexing errors; browse originals when searches fail.
6. **Adjoining counties** (Berks, Carbon, Columbia, Dauphin, Lebanon, Luzerne, Northumberland) — families near any border may have records on both sides.

---

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811, carved from Berks and Northampton Counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this place and period; no verified figures can be stated.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated the period absolutely. The county held the heart of the Pennsylvania anthracite region; collieries, breakers, ironworks, and the Reading Railroad all operated here. Subsidiary trades (blacksmiths, teamsters, merchants, boarding house keepers) clustered around the mining patches.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Welsh and English mining communities established by the 1840s, followed by heavy Irish immigration especially after the Famine (post-1847), then Germans. By the late 1870s significant influxes of Poles, Lithuanians, and Slavic miners were beginning.
- **Religious denominations:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Welsh Baptist, Episcopal, Roman Catholic (Irish and later Polish), Lutheran (German), Reformed (German), Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian.
- **Key historical events:** Canal era (Schuylkill Canal) gave way to railroad dominance (Philadelphia and Reading Railroad). The Molly Maguires trials (1875–1877) produced extensive court records. The Civil War (1861–1865) drew heavily from the county's labor force.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton Counties. Its boundaries were stable throughout the 1840–1880 period.
- Records predating 1811 for this territory fall under Berks County (southern portion) and Northampton County (northern portion).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records did not return jurisdiction-specific content in this run. Pennsylvania statewide civil registration is broadly known to have begun in 1893, but no specific earlier local or county-level requirement can be cited from tool results.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch has one digitized volume of marriage records (imageGroupNumber 007936753, 94 images, 1870–1910) — browse-only, 0% indexed.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse; Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death records exist as a class for 1840–1880. Marriage records at the courthouse may predate 1870 but are not digitized for earlier years.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the primary vital record source.
- **Digitization level:** Marriage records — browse-only images.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Welsh Baptist, Roman Catholic, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian, Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized volume 007936751 (187 images, 1842–1895), browse-only, English and German. Collections_search also returned SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (verify before use).
- **Language:** English and German; Welsh-congregation registers may be in Welsh.
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 available. Ancestry has a curated 1850 Schuylkill County collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/). Mortality schedules 1850–1880 available.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct regular state censuses.
- **Other enumerations:** Annual tax assessment lists serve as intercensal substitutes.
- **Access:** Federal census indexed and imaged on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). 1870 census has known indexing errors.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, orphans' court.
- **Date range:** From 1811 onward. FamilySearch volume 007936749 (412 images, 1851–1930) covers 1851–1880 of the target period. Collection 1999196 (3,200,560 images, 1683–1994) has images but no name index.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse; FamilySearch browse-only images.
- **Naturalization records:** Volume 007936750 (298 images, 1849–1915), browse-only.

Subsidiary trades (blacksmiths, teamsters, merchants, boarding house keepers) clustered around the mining patches.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Welsh and English mining communities established by the 1840s; heavy Irish immigration after the Famine (post-1847); Germans; and by the late 1870s, growing influxes of Polish, Lithuanian, and Slavic miners.
- **Religious denominations:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Welsh Baptist, Episcopal, Roman Catholic (Irish and later Polish), Lutheran (German), Reformed (German), Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian.
- **Key historical events:** The Schuylkill Canal gave way to railroad dominance (Philadelphia and Reading Railroad). The Molly Maguires trials (1875–1877) produced extensive court records. The Civil War (1861–1865) drew heavily from the county's labor force, including the 48th Pennsylvania Infantry raised largely from miners.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton Counties; **county seat:** Pottsville
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated, with the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad moving coal east. Large iron foundries and commercial sectors also present.
- **Ethnic composition:** Welsh, Irish (large post-Famine influx after 1847), German, and English immigrant populations concentrated in mining patches.
- **Denominations:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Roman Catholic, Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist Episcopal, and Anglican.

---

## Vital Records (Civil Registration)

Pennsylvania **did not have statewide civil registration** during the 1840s–1860s — births, marriages, and deaths were not systematically recorded at any government level. Church records are the primary alternative for vital events. The county courthouse may hold some marriage bonds and licenses.

---

## Census Records

The most accessible and best-indexed record type for this period.

| Census | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870 federal census | All of Schuylkill County | FamilySearch (1850–1860 volume, 96% name-indexed, full-text searchable, 412 images) |
| 1850 U.S. Federal Census | Schuylkill County | Ancestry.com (indexed) |

**Mortality schedules** (1850, 1860) recorded deaths in the year preceding each census — these are the closest substitute for death records in this era and are highly valuable.

---

## Church Records

- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Lutheran church records, 1840–1875 (image group 004288771, 198 images). **Browse-only, not name-indexed**, bilingual English/German — must be read page by page.
- **Other denominations** (Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Roman Catholic, German Reformed, Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian) hold records at originating parishes or diocesan archives — most are **not digitized**.
- **Language note:** Lutheran and German Reformed records may be partly or entirely in German.

---

## Probate & Court Records

- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Schuylkill County probate records, 1845–1880 (image group 004812990, 286 images). Only 4% name-indexed, but **full-text searchable**.
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianship files, estate inventories, and distribution records.
- **Naturalizations:** Immigrant miners (Irish, Welsh, German) filed naturalization petitions at the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas — a critical source for immigrant families.
- **Physical records:** Complete probate and court files at the Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville.

---

## Land Records

- Pennsylvania is a **state-land (metes and bounds) state** — no federal land patents apply. By the 1840s–1860s, most transactions were private deeds recorded at the county level.
- **Deed books** and grantor/grantee indexes: Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville.
- **Warrants and patents:** Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.
- **Tax records** (real and personal property, assessed at township level) survive in varying completeness and can track an ancestor year-to-year between censuses.

---

## Military Records

- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Compiled service records and pension files at NARA; state service records at Pennsylvania State Archives. Civil War draft registration (1863) indexed on Ancestry and Fold3.
- **Mexican-American War (1846–1848):** Bounty land warrants at NARA.

---

## Newspapers

- **Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, est. 1825): The primary local paper throughout this period. Obituaries frequently name family members, birthplaces, and immigrant origins — invaluable given the absence of civil vital records.
- Partial runs available on **Chronicling America** (free); microfilm at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.

---

## Immigration Records

- **Primary ports:** Philadelphia (Welsh, Irish, German immigrants); Baltimore (German immigrants).
- Philadelphia passenger arrival lists (post-1840) are detailed and often name the immigrant's hometown. Check **Ancestry** and **FamilySearch**.
- Naturalization petitions at the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas complement passenger records.

---

## Occupational Records

- **Coal company records:** Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company employment records survive for parts of this period at the **Hagley Museum and Library** (Wilmington, DE) — names employees with age and nationality.
- City directories for Pottsville (intercensal years) held at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1850–1860 census (96% indexed, 412 images); probate 1845–1880 (full-text, 286 images); Lutheran church records 1840–1875 (browse-only, 198 images) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 U.S. Federal Census — Schuylkill County | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Partial runs of the Miners' Journal and other PA papers | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, probate records, court minute books, naturalization records |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land warrants and patents, military records |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville | Local histories, newspaper microfilm, cemetery transcriptions |
| Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington, DE | Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company records |
| NARA Philadelphia Regional | Civil War records, draft records, passenger lists |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia | Presbyterian church records for Pennsylvania |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the census.** The 1850 and 1860 federal censuses are well-indexed and free on FamilySearch. Use the mortality schedule from the same census year to document deaths in the preceding year.
2. **No civil registration exists** — identify your ancestor's denomination before searching for baptisms, marriages, and burials. Lutheran and German Reformed records may be in German.
3. **The Miners' Journal is underused.** Obituaries and death notices are the practical substitute for death certificates in this era.
4. **For immigrants:** Search Philadelphia passenger arrival lists (Ancestry) *and* the naturalization records at the Pottsville courthouse. The post-1847 Irish wave and the Welsh immigration streams are well represented.
5. **Probate records are full-text searchable** on FamilySearch despite low name-indexing — run a text search before browsing images.
6. **Coal company employment records** at Hagley are worth a visit or inquiry for any ancestor who was a miner — they can confirm names, ages, and national origins otherwise undocumented.
7. **Check adjacent counties** (Berks, Carbon, Lebanon, Northumberland, Luzerne) — families near borders frequently generated records on both sides.
8. **Pre-1811 records** for territory now in Schuylkill County are held by Berks County (southeastern portions) and Northampton County (northeastern portions).

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811, carved from Berks and Northampton Counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query (a coverage gap in that tool's data for this county). Schuylkill County was one of Pennsylvania's fastest-growing counties in this era, driven almost entirely by anthracite coal extraction.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated — Pottsville and Minersville were major mining towns. Railroads (particularly the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad) moved coal east. Subsidiary industries included iron foundries and a significant retail and commercial sector serving miners.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Welsh, Irish (particularly post-Famine Irish after 1847), German, and English immigrant populations concentrated in the mining patches. The Welsh and English arrived earliest; German settlers were common in the agricultural northern and western townships.
- **Religious denominations:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist (Congregational), Anglican/Episcopal, Roman Catholic (serving Irish and later Welsh immigrants), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, and Methodist Episcopal congregations were all present. German Lutheran congregations were particularly active in rural townships.
- **Key historical events:** Rapid coal-driven population growth; the "Long Strike" of 1858; Civil War service (1861–1865) and the Molly Maguires era beginning in the late 1860s. The county produced significant Union Army enlistments.

## Boundary changes

Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton Counties. Its boundaries were stable through the 1840s–1860s target period — no subdivision or boundary change occurred during these decades. Records generated in this period belong entirely to Schuylkill County. Pre-1811 records for territory within present Schuylkill County are held by Berks County (eastern/southeastern portions) and Northampton County (northeastern portions).

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not have statewide civil registration during the 1840s–1860s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records and Schuylkill County both redirected to a generic article and returned no Pennsylvania-specific registration date. Based on that gap: the FamilySearch Wiki does not confirm a specific statewide start date for this tool run. It is well established in the research literature that Pennsylvania's statewide civil registration system began in 1906 — but because that date did not appear in any tool result returned in this session, I am flagging it as unconfirmed from this survey's sources rather than asserting it as a finding.
- **What this means for 1840s–1860s:** There was no statewide civil registration in Pennsylvania during this period. Vital events were not systematically registered at any government level. There is no county-level civil vital records series to search for births, marriages, or deaths in this era.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials. Marriage bonds and licenses were sometimes kept at the county level; check the Schuylkill County courthouse records. Death notices in local newspapers are another significant source (see Newspaper records below).

### Church records

- **What FamilySearch holds:** `collections_search` returned a collection titled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (collection ID: SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, date range 1708–1985), reported at approximately 1.2 million records, 982,000 person entries, and 607,000 images. **Note:** this collection carries a "synthetic test fixture" identifier in the tool data, which means it is a test/placeholder entry and does not represent a verified live FamilySearch collection. Do not treat its record counts as confirmed. Treat this as a gap pending direct verification at FamilySearch.org.
- **Confirmed digitized volumes:** `volume_search` returned one digitized volume of Schuylkill County Lutheran church records (image group 004288771, 198 images, covering 1840–1875). This volume is in English and German, has **0% name-indexing** and is **not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image. Researchers must be able to read German to use the German-language entries.
- **Denominations present:** Lutheran and German Reformed congregations were numerous in the rural townships and produced records in German. Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Anglican, Roman Catholic, Methodist Episcopal, and Presbyterian congregations also served the county, particularly in the mining towns.
- **Where held:** Local parishes and denominational archives hold originals. FamilySearch has at least one digitized browse-only volume (Lutheran, 1840–1875). The Pennsylvania State Archives and the Presbyterian Historical Society in Philadelphia hold additional denominational records.
- **Access level:** Browse-only images (Lutheran volume); physical or microfilm for most other denominations.
- **Language:** German for Lutheran and German Reformed records; English for most others.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1840, 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal censuses all covered Schuylkill County. `volume_search` returned a digitized volume (image group 007621224, 412 images) covering the 1850–1860 census for Schuylkill County. This volume is **96% name-indexed** and **full-text searchable** — the most accessible record type in this survey.
- **Ancestry.com** also holds the 1850 United States Federal Census for Schuylkill County (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/), confirmed by `external_links_search`.
- **Mortality schedules:** The federal mortality schedules (1850, 1860, 1870) recorded deaths in the year preceding each census. These are the closest substitute for death records during this period and are highly valuable for the 1840s–1860s.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period — no state-level intercensal enumeration exists.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (1850–1860 federal census on FamilySearch and Ancestry); browse or physical for 1840 and 1870.

### Probate and court records

- **What FamilySearch holds:** `collections_search` returned "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection ID: 1999196) with 3.2 million images but 0 indexed records — the collection is image-only, not name-searchable. `volume_search` also returned a separate digitized volume of Schuylkill County probate records (image group 004812990, 286 images, covering 1845–1880). This volume is only **4% name-indexed** but is **full-text searchable**, meaning you can search its text but most entries are not linked to person profiles.
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianship files, estate inventories, and distribution records. For an ancestor who died intestate, search administrations; for one who left a will, search the will books.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse in Pottsville (Register of Wills office). FamilySearch has a digitized partial volume (1845–1880, 286 images).
- **Court records:** Naturalizations for immigrants (Irish, Welsh, German miners) were filed at the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas. These are a critical source for the immigrant mining population. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; check county court minute books as well as formal naturalization records.
- **Access level:** Full-text searchable but largely not name-indexed (FamilySearch); physical records at the Pottsville courthouse for complete coverage.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state (metes and bounds), not a public-land state. The Penn family originally granted land; after the Revolution, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania issued warrants and patents. By the 1840s–1860s, most land transactions were private deeds recorded at the county level.
- **Types:** Deed books (grantor/grantee indexes at the county courthouse), warrants and patents (Pennsylvania State Archives), mortgages, and tax records. Mining leases and coal company land records are particularly significant for this county.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds in Pottsville for deed books. Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg for warrants and patents.
- **Digitization:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Land and Property redirected to a generic article, so no digitization status was confirmed from this survey's sources. Check FamilySearch.org and Ancestry directly.
- **Tax records:** Property tax and personal property tax records were kept at the township level and survive in varying completeness. These substitute for census records in off-census years and can help track an ancestor's residence year by year.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Mexican-American War (1846–1848) drew some Schuylkill County men. The Civil War (1861–1865) is the dominant military source for this period — Schuylkill County contributed significantly to Pennsylvania volunteer infantry and cavalry regiments.
- **Record types:** Civil War compiled service records and pension files at NARA (National Archives and Records Administration, Washington D.C.). Pennsylvania's adjutant general compiled state service records, held at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Civil War draft registration records (1863) are at NARA and are searchable through Ancestry and Fold3.
- **Bounty land warrants:** Issued for Mexican War service (not Civil War). At NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA for federal records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state records; Ancestry and Fold3 for digital access.
- **Access level:** Civil War draft records are indexed and online. Compiled service records are available via NARA or Fold3 (subscription).

### Cemetery records

- **Coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves both cover Schuylkill County cemeteries, though coverage is volunteer-driven and incomplete. Mining communities had numerous small patch-town cemeteries associated with specific ethnic or denominational groups.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for larger cemeteries may survive at the cemetery office or with the sponsoring church.
- **Note:** The mortality schedules (1850, 1860) are a strong complement to cemetery research since they record deaths the year before the census was taken.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville) began publication in 1825 and ran continuously through the target period. It is a major source for obituaries, marriage notices, mining accident reports, and legal notices. Other papers included the Pottsville Emporium and the Schuylkill Haven Sentinel.
- **Where held:** The Miners' Journal is partially digitized — check Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free) and newspaper archive sites. The Schuylkill County Historical Society holds microfilm runs.
- **Content value:** Obituaries in the Miners' Journal frequently name family members, birthplaces, and immigrant origins — critically valuable given the absence of civil vital records in this period.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary arrival port for Welsh, Irish, and German immigrants coming to Schuylkill County in the 1840s–1860s. Baltimore was a secondary port, particularly for German immigrants.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at Philadelphia (indexed at Ancestry and FamilySearch), naturalization petitions at the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas, and declarations of intention. Post-1840 Philadelphia passenger lists are detailed and often name the immigrant's home town.
- **Important note:** Examine full passenger manifests for entire families — infants and young children are listed alongside parents. A family that immigrated together will all appear on the same manifest entry.
- **Where held:** NARA for original manifests; Ancestry and FamilySearch for digital access.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images for Philadelphia arrivals on Ancestry; FamilySearch has partial indexing.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Real and personal property tax records assessed at the township level in Schuylkill County. Poll taxes were also collected.
- **Value as a substitute:** Tax lists exist for most years in the 1840s–1860s and can place an ancestor in a specific township in years between censuses, track property acquisition, and identify relatives living in proximity.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse and the Pennsylvania State Archives. The Historical Society of Schuylkill County may hold additional runs.

### Other record types

- **Occupational records:** Coal mine employment records, particularly from the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, survive for parts of this period and are held at the Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, Delaware) and the Reading Railroad Historical and Technical Society. These name employees by name and sometimes give age and nationality.
- **Court minute books:** The Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas minute books record road assignments, poor relief, guardian appointments, and county business that names ordinary residents who never appeared in any other court proceeding.
- **City directories:** Pottsville directories exist for portions of this era and can place residents at specific addresses in intercensal years. Check the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.

## Records NOT online

- Most church records other than the single Lutheran volume on FamilySearch (1840–1875) are not digitized or online. Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Roman Catholic (pre-1870 especially), German Reformed, and Methodist Episcopal registers must be sought at the originating parish or diocesan archives.
- County deed books and grantor/grantee indexes are not confirmed as online for this period — check the county recorder's office directly.
- Court of Common Pleas minute books, beyond what is captured in the probate volume, are physical records at the courthouse.
- Most tax records are physical only, at the courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.

No specific courthouse fires or record losses for Schuylkill County in the 1840s–1860s were identified in the tool results returned during this survey. **Note:** All four sections of the FamilySearch Wiki place pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) — attempted at both the county and state level — returned the same generic fallback article rather than Pennsylvania- or Schuylkill-specific content. - https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy
- https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records

**From tool results actually returned in this session:**

- The federal census is the most accessible and best-indexed record type for this period. Start there for 1850 and 1860 — the FamilySearch volume (007621224) is 96% indexed and full-text searchable. Use the mortality schedule from the same census year to document deaths.
- There was no civil vital registration in Pennsylvania during the 1840s–1860s. Church records are the only systematic source for births, marriages, and burials. Identify the denomination before searching, and note that Lutheran and German Reformed records may be partly or entirely in German.
- The single Lutheran church records volume on FamilySearch (image group 004288771, 1840–1875) is browse-only and bilingual (English/German). Budget time to browse it page by page.
- The probate records volume on FamilySearch (004812990, 1845–1880) is full-text searchable but only 4% name-indexed. Use the full-text search first; if that fails, browse the images directly.
- Schuylkill County had very large Irish and Welsh immigrant populations from the 1840s onward. For these families, search Philadelphia passenger arrival lists (Ancestry) and the Schuylkill County naturalization records at the courthouse. The Miners' Journal often published notices when prominent miners died or when immigrant groups arrived.
- Pennsylvania is a state-land (metes and bounds) state. There are no federal land patents for Schuylkill County — all land distribution went through the Commonwealth. Deed books at the Pottsville courthouse are the primary land record.
- For Civil War–era research (1861–1865), check both NARA compiled service records and the Pennsylvania State Archives adjutant general records, as the two series complement each other.
- Neighboring counties — Berks to the south, Lebanon to the west, Dauphin and Northumberland to the northwest, Columbia and Luzerne to the north, and Carbon to the east — share borders with Schuylkill. Families near those borders likely generated records in adjacent counties as well. The FamilySearch Wiki county genealogy page (which returned only generic content in this session) would normally list the neighboring counties table; researchers should check that page directly for confirmation.

For the 1840s–1860s themselves, the county's own tax assessments are the relevant series.

Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania in the 1840s–1860s was a booming anthracite coal county with large Welsh, Irish, and German immigrant communities. There was no government registration of births, marriages, or deaths during this period, so church records and census records carry the most weight — the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses are well-indexed and available free on FamilySearch, while church records (particularly Lutheran ones) survive in a browse-only digitized volume that requires reading some German. Probate records and the Miners' Journal newspaper are the other strong sources. Most other records — deed books, court files, coal company employment rolls, and most church registers — exist only on paper at the Pottsville courthouse, the Pennsylvania State Archives, or local repositories. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania and Schuylkill County returned only generic content during this survey, so researchers should visit those pages directly for jurisdiction-specific guidance.

The natural next step is to build a research plan: once you have a specific ancestor in mind, the census, the Miners' Journal, and the Philadelphia passenger lists are the three places to start.

---

**Locality Guide saved as `loc_001`**

**Pulaski County, Kentucky — 1840–1880 Survey**

Pulaski County's seat is **Somerset**; the county has existed since 1798 (formed from Lincoln and Green counties). Two major research challenges:

1. **Courthouse fires** (1838 and 1871) destroyed unknown portions of early records.
2. **No reliable civil vital registration** — birth and death registers are largely absent for this entire window.

**What survives and where:**

- **Marriage bonds** — from 1799 (most complete series); records through 1871 are digitized online.
- **Will books** — through 1929 are digitized online.
- **Church records** (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian) — the primary source for births and deaths; the Pulaski County Historical Society in Somerset holds the best local collection of church records and obituaries.
- **Federal censuses** — all five census years (1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) are indexed on both Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Annual tax lists** — essential for filling gaps between censuses (Kentucky held no state census).
- **Civil War records** — search both Union records at NARA and Confederate pension records at the Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA).

---

**⚠️ Important note:** The subagent was only able to survey **Pulaski County** in this session. **Greenup County** and **Boyd County** each need to be run as separate locality-guide requests. Please ask for those individually to get their full surveys.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (circa 1790–1820)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Alabama achieved statehood on 14 December 1819. Around 1800, the territory fell under two successive federal jurisdictions: the **Mississippi Territory** (established 1798, reorganized 1817) and then the **Alabama Territory** (1817–1819). Critically, the **Mobile area remained a Spanish colonial outpost until 1813**, when US forces seized it.

**Early Alabama counties:** Washington (1800), Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), Mobile (1813).

---

## The Most Important Thing to Know First: Jurisdiction Split

Records for circa-1800 Alabama do **not** exist in Alabama state archives — they are **Mississippi Territory records**. Begin at both ADAH and MDAH simultaneously; neither alone holds the full picture.

If your ancestor was **near Mobile**, their records before 1813 are **Spanish colonial**, not American. Do not expect to find them in US-system archives for that period.

---

## Available Record Types

### Census Records
- The **1810 federal census** is your earliest reliable American population record for most of Alabama. The 1800 census covered only sparse settlements.
- The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** that included settlers in present-day Alabama — held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH).
- **FamilySearch:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (collection 2016756, index only, no images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756

### Marriage Records
- No civil vital registration existed at the county or territorial level for circa 1800.
- Marriage records begin county-by-county after county formation (1800+).
- **FamilySearch:** "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (collection 1598408): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408

### Church Records
- **Catholic (Mobile):** Continuous from 1702 — baptisms, marriages, burials. Held at the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives and Mobile Municipal Archives. French-era in French; Spanish-era in Spanish.
- **Methodist/Baptist (interior):** Circuit riders from the 1790s onward. Scattered among denominational archives.
- **FamilySearch:** "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (collection 1986396, images available): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396

### Probate and Court Records
- Washington County (formed 1800) has the earliest Alabama-area probate records.
- **FamilySearch:** "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (collection 1537764, images available): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764
- **Browse-only digitized volumes** (no name index, must browse image by image):
  - Volume 004512889: Territorial court and land records, 1808–1819 (214 images)
  - Volume 004512890: Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820 (96 images)

### Land Records
- Alabama is a **federal land state** — the GLO survey system applies.
- Federal patents: **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) — free online.
- Spanish colonial land grants (Mobile, pre-1813): Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at the Library of Congress.
- Tax lists (from county formation) are a critical substitute for sparse census coverage.

### Military Records
- Creek War (1813–1814), War of 1812.
- Service records and pension files at **NARA, Washington DC**; many digitized on **Fold3** (fold3.com).
- Territorial militia rolls may be at ADAH and MDAH.

### Spanish Colonial Records (Mobile, pre-1813)
- Padrones (population counts), land grants, church registers.
- **Archivo General de Indias, Seville** — written request; microfilm at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What's Here | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Marriages 1809+, Probate 1809+, Census 1810+, Church 1803+, 2 browse-only territorial volumes | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal censuses (1800, 1810); additional Alabama collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Creek War & War of 1812 military records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| Chronicling America (loc.gov) | Early territorial newspapers | Free |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery** | Territorial censuses 1801–1808; territorial tax lists; state records from 1819; county records microfilm |
| **Mississippi Dept. of Archives and History (MDAH), Jackson** | Mississippi Territory records (Washington County and Alabama-area counties pre-1817) |
| **NARA, Washington DC** | Federal land patents; military service/pension records; federal census originals |
| **Library of Congress** | Copies of Spanish colonial Mobile records; French colonial microfilm; early newspapers |
| **Archdiocese of Mobile Archives** | Catholic parish registers from 1702 |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | French colonial records microfilm; local historical records |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville** | Spanish colonial land grants, padrones, church records for Mobile district |
| **County courthouses** | Deed books, probate, court minutes from county formation |

---

## Records NOT Online

- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 — physical at ADAH; not confirmed digitized.
- Spanish colonial padrones and land grants for Mobile — physical in Seville; copies at Library of Congress; not searchable by name online.
- French colonial records — microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives only.
- Territorial tax lists (pre-1809) — physical at ADAH and county courthouses.
- Catholic parish registers for Mobile before 1813 — physical at Archdiocese of Mobile; not confirmed indexed online.
- Two browse-only FamilySearch volumes (004512889, 004512890) — images available but 0% name-indexed; must be browsed page by page.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Determine location first.** Mobile coastal area (Spanish records, different language and repository) vs. interior/Tennessee River valley (American territorial records) requires completely different strategies.
2. **The 1810 census is your earliest solid anchor.** Use territorial tax lists (1800–1809) to track presence between censuses.
3. **Land records are the richest source for this period.** Federal patents, Spanish grants, and deed books often give origin, neighbors, and approximate arrival date — use cluster research to follow neighbors from their Carolina/Virginia/Georgia origins.
4. **Visit the FamilySearch Wiki directly** at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy for the full current page — some Alabama-specific sections could not be retrieved by automated tools during this survey.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (circa 1790–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood 14 December 1819. At and around 1800, the territory was under two successive federal jurisdictions: the Mississippi Territory (established 1798, reorganized 1817) and then the Alabama Territory (1817–1819). The Mobile area remained a Spanish colonial outpost until 1813, when US forces seized it.
- **County seat / administrative center:** The territorial capital was first at Natchez (Mississippi side), then Washington, Mississippi. Present-day Alabama's earliest American counties — Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), Washington (1800), and Mobile (1813) — had their own county seats.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned for this period by the population tool. The Wikipedia extract notes that settlement was sparse before the Creek War of 1813–1814, concentrated near Mobile Bay and the Tennessee River valley. The Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in what is now Alabama, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton agriculture, fur trade, and Spanish colonial trade through Mobile port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Euro-American settlers arriving from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia; Spanish and French creole communities around Mobile; Creek, Cherokee, and Choctaw nations throughout the interior.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant in Mobile under French and Spanish eras); Methodist and Baptist circuits followed settlers from the Carolinas and Virginia into the interior.
- **Key historical events:** French founding of Mobile (1702); transfer to Britain (1763); Spanish control (1780–1813); creation of Mississippi Territory (1798); Creek War (1813–1814), which opened much of central Alabama to American settlement; Alabama statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes

This is the most important factor for this period. The territory that is now Alabama passed through three distinct governing authorities:

- **Before 1780:** The Mobile area was French (1702–1763), then British (1763–1780). Records from this era are colonial, not American.
- **1780–1813:** Mobile and its district were Spanish. Records were created under Spanish colonial administration.
- **1798–1817:** The remainder of present-day Alabama (outside Mobile) fell under the Mississippi Territory. Washington County (created 1800) was the first county covering much of what is now southern Alabama; Madison County (1808) covered the northern Tennessee River valley.
- **1813:** US forces occupied Mobile; it became part of the Mississippi Territory.
- **1817–1819:** The Alabama Territory was carved from the eastern half of the Mississippi Territory.

**Critical rule:** Records before 1813 for the Mobile area will be found in Spanish colonial archives, not American ones. Records before 1798 for the interior are effectively non-existent in the American record system. Records created 1798–1817 are Mississippi Territory records, not Alabama state records — search under Washington County, Mississippi Territory or Madison County, Mississippi Territory as appropriate.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Alabama did not have statewide civil registration of births and deaths during this period. The FamilySearch Alabama Genealogy wiki page was not retrievable in full (the wiki_read tool returned only a generic fallback for Alabama-specific URLs — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Vital_Records directly). No specific registration date can be stated from the tools for this period.
- **What exists:** No civil birth or death registration existed at the county or territorial level for circa 1800. Marriage records begin county-by-county after county formation: the FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (collection 1598408) is the earliest indexed marriage series for Alabama, starting 1809. https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408
- **Where held:** County courthouses for their respective counties; digitized marriages searchable on FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** No civil vital registration of births or deaths for this period. The Mobile area's pre-1813 vital events were registered in the Catholic parish.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers for Mobile; Methodist and Baptist circuit records for the interior (where they survive).

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, continuous from 1702); Methodist and Baptist (interior, circuit riders arriving from the 1790s onward).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic); membership rolls (Methodist, Baptist).
- **Where held:** Catholic records for Mobile are held at the Archdiocese of Mobile and at the Mobile Municipal Archives, which also holds French colonial microfilm per the wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records. Spanish colonial church registers for the Mobile district are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress, per that same source. FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (collection 1986396, 156,789 records, images available) covers some of this: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French era are in French; Spanish era records are in Spanish. Early American Baptist/Methodist records are in English.

### Census records

- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that included settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery, per the wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records.
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census is the first to enumerate what would become Alabama in its present boundaries. The 1800 federal census covered only the very sparse settlements in the Mississippi Territory's Alabama portion.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (collection 2016756, 287,634 records, index only, no images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756. Note the starting date of 1810 — the territorial censuses of 1801–1808 are not in this collection and must be sought at ADAH or through other finding aids.
- **Access:** The 1810 federal census is indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Territorial censuses of 1801–1808 are not confirmed as digitized by the tools; consult ADAH directly.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories — filed at county level after county formation.
- **Date range:** Washington County (formed 1800) has the earliest Alabama-area probate records; Madison County from 1808.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (collection 1537764, 438,210 records, images available): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764. Note the 1809 start date — anything before 1809 is not in this indexed collection.
- **Digitized volumes:** FamilySearch volume search returned 2 browse-only digitized volumes for the period 1780–1820:
  - Volume 004512889 (214 images): Territorial court and land records, Alabama, 1808–1819. Browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
  - Volume 004512890 (96 images): Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820. Browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
  Both volumes must be browsed image by image with no name search capability.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state — the General Land Office (GLO) survey system applies. Land grants and patents were issued by the federal government through the GLO.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The US General Land Office issued patents for federal land in the Mississippi and Alabama territories. The BLM GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal land patent records. For the Mobile area before 1813, land grants were issued by the Spanish colonial government.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish colonial land grants, territorial-era deed books (county level), tax lists.
- **Date range:** Federal patents begin after the land was formally surveyed and opened, which for Alabama's interior was primarily after 1800 and especially after 1814. Spanish land grants in Mobile predate 1813.
- **Where held:** Federal patents: BLM GLO Records website. Spanish land grants: Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Library of Congress copies, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records. County-level deeds: county courthouses and FamilySearch digitized volumes (see Volume 004512890 above for Washington County, browse-only).
- **French and British colonial grants:** French colonial land records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives, per the same wiki_search source.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812 (which included action in the Mobile area).
- **Record types:** Militia rolls (territorial period), service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** Federal service records and pension files are at NARA in Washington, DC. Territorial militia records and Mississippi Territory militia rolls may be at ADAH and the Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH). Fold3 (fold3.com) hosts many digitized NARA military records.
- **Note:** Bounty land warrants were issued after the Creek War and War of 1812 and may document family relationships.

### Cemetery records

- **Where held:** Major online coverage is through FindAGrave (findagrave.com), which covers Alabama cemeteries. Physical sexton records for this early period are rare and generally not online.
- **Note:** Many burials from circa 1800 were in family cemeteries on private land with no formal records.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Mobile had a Spanish-era gazette; American newspapers in the territory were sparse before 1815. Consult the Library of Congress Chronicling America database (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) for early territorial newspapers.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sales, arrival notices — useful for tracing movement.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was an active port from the French era. New Orleans (Louisiana) was the major nearby port.
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial arrival records for Mobile; US passenger lists after 1813. Many settlers arrived overland from Georgia and the Carolinas, not by sea — no port arrival record will exist for them.
- **Where held:** NARA for US-era passenger lists. Spanish colonial Mobile records at the Archivo General de Indias and Library of Congress copies.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants. When researching a family arriving by sea at Mobile or New Orleans, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial tax lists exist for some Mississippi Territory counties covering present-day Alabama.
- **Date range:** From county formation — Washington County from 1800, Madison County from 1808.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial-era tax records. Some have been published or microfilmed.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are a critical substitute for the sparse census coverage before 1810, and for the non-enumerating years between territorial censuses.

### Other record types

- **Spanish colonial census records (padrones):** The Spanish conducted periodic population counts (padrones) of the Mobile district. These are held in Seville and at the Library of Congress, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **Indian land cession records:** Treaties and land cession agreements with the Creek, Cherokee, and Choctaw nations name tribal members and may name Euro-American traders or agents who intermarried. These are at NARA.
- **Town and county histories:** Published county histories (19th-century) frequently transcribe early records and list founding families. WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog are the best finding aids for these.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages 1809–1950 (612,345 records); Alabama, Probate Records 1809–1985 (438,210 records, images); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810–1890 (287,634 records, index only); Alabama, Church Records 1803–1950 (156,789 records, images); 2 browse-only digitized territorial volumes (1803–1820) | Free |

- **The jurisdiction split is the most important starting point.** Records for circa 1800 Alabama do not exist in Alabama state archives — they are Mississippi Territory records. Here is the locality guide the agent produced:

---

**Arkansas Region before 1800 (Spanish Colonial Period, 1763–1803)**

**Overview**

Because no American county system, civil registration, or federal census existed during this period, surviving records are colonial in character. The Arkansas Post settlement dates to 1686 (French), and Spain took control of the territory in 1763. The Louisiana Purchase in 1803 ended the Spanish era.

**Key Record Types**

| Record Type | What It Contains | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **Catholic sacramental registers** | Baptisms, marriages, burials kept by French missionaries at Arkansas Post | Arkansas History Commission; Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock; FamilySearch (image group **008814402** — 64 images, browse-only, in Spanish, *no name index*) |
| **Padrones (Spanish household censuses)** | Head of household, household members, sometimes ages | Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Arkansas History Commission (microfilm) |
| **Spanish land concessions** | Land grants by the Spanish Crown naming the grantee | Archivo General de Indias; BLM General Land Office records (some U.S. patents trace back to Spanish grants) |
| **Military garrison records** | Soldiers stationed at Arkansas Post | Archivo General de Indias, Seville |

**Key Repositories**

1. **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) — primary U.S. repository for colonial Arkansas materials; holds microfilm of Spanish-era records.
2. **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) — the central colonial archive; partially browsable free online through Spain's [PARES portal](https://pares.mcu.es).
3. **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** — holds original or copies of the Arkansas Post Catholic registers.
4. **FamilySearch** — one digitized volume (image group 008814402) requires manual page-by-page browsing; no index exists.

**Most Practical Starting Point**

Search the **BLM General Land Office** records at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) for any confirmed U.S. land patent tracing back to a Spanish-era grant. This will name the ancestor and give you a foothold before approaching the Seville archives.

---

This entry has been saved to your project as **loc_001**. The FamilySearch volume will need to be browsed image by image (use the `search-images` skill), and any Spanish-language documents will likely need translation assistance.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

Ohio in 1790 was part of the **Northwest Territory**, created by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. It didn't become a state until **1 March 1803**. Settlement was sparse, government was new, and church infrastructure barely existed — meaning many events simply generated *no written record at all*, not that records were lost.

---

## Boundary Changes

This is the most critical issue for 1790 research:

- **1788:** Washington County organized — covered all of eastern Ohio (east of the Scioto River).
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized — covered all of western Ohio (west of the Scioto River).
- **After 1790:** Counties were rapidly carved from these two as settlement expanded.

**Key rule:** Any 1790 Ohio event was recorded — if at all — under **Washington County** or **Hamilton County** only. Never search a post-1803 county name for a 1790 event.

---

## Available Records

### What does NOT exist in 1790
- **No civil vital records** — Ohio didn't establish statewide civil registration until 1908.
- **No federal census** — the 1790 census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory. The **1800 census is the earliest** federal enumeration for Ohio.
- **No Ohio newspapers** — the first appeared in Cincinnati in 1793.

### What does exist

| Record Type | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **County Marriages (from 1789)** | FamilySearch collection 1803785; 1.5M records | Free online |

| **Revolutionary War pension files** | Often the richest source: autobiographical life histories naming family members and migration routes | Fold3 / NARA |
