entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Era), 1780-1810

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, covering present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. Ohio became the first state carved from it on 1 March 1803.
- **Administrative center:** Marietta (territorial capital); Columbus became the state capital in 1816.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory (federal), administered by the U.S. Congress under the Ordinance of 1787.
- **Population during period:** Population data returned no figures for this period from place_population — the region had very sparse Euro-American settlement in 1790. The 1800 federal census (the first to enumerate Ohio) counted approximately 45,000 residents in Washington and Hamilton counties.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, military garrison supply. The Ohio River was the primary migration and commerce corridor.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American settlers arriving from Virginia, Pennsylvania, New England, and Kentucky; significant Indigenous nations (Shawnee, Delaware/Lenape, Wyandot, Miami) whose own records are held separately in federal treaty and Indian agent records.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist itinerants, Presbyterian and Baptist missionaries were the earliest organized denominations. Quaker settlers arrived in the southeastern region. Catholic missionaries operated in some areas. Formal church structures were sparse in 1790.
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris 1783 opened the region to American settlement; Northwest Ordinance 1787 established governance; Battle of Fallen Timbers 1794 and Treaty of Greenville 1795 dramatically shifted the settler-Indigenous boundary and opened most of Ohio to settlement.

## Boundary changes
- **1787:** Northwest Ordinance creates the Northwest Territory — the entire future state of Ohio falls under this single territorial jurisdiction with no county subdivisions.
- **1788:** Washington County organized as the first county — covered all of present-day Ohio east of the Scioto River and south of Lake Erie.
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized — covered all of present-day Ohio west of the Scioto River.
- **1796 onward:** Additional counties carved rapidly from Washington and Hamilton counties as settlement expanded. Researchers must consult a boundary atlas to determine the correct county for any event before statehood.
- **1803:** Ohio achieves statehood. Records shift from territorial to state-level jurisdiction. Court of Common Pleas replaces territorial courts.
- **Key rule:** Any event in Ohio in 1790 was recorded (if at all) under Washington County or Hamilton County jurisdiction, depending on which side of the Scioto River the location falls. Never search a post-1803 county name for a 1790 event.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Ohio did not require civil registration of births and deaths at the statewide level until 1908. The FamilySearch Wiki specific Ohio Vital Records page did not return — generic content only was returned by that URL. No county-level civil registration date for the territorial period was found in tool results.
- **What exists for 1790:** No civil vital records exist for this period. Births, marriages, and deaths in 1790 were not registered by any government in the Northwest Territory.
- **Marriage records:** The FamilySearch collection 'Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013' (id: 1803785; 1,523,678 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) begins in 1789 and covers county-level marriage bonds and licenses. This is the earliest civil marriage record series available. Digitization level: indexed + images.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the only source for baptisms, marriages, and burials in 1790.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker (Society of Friends), and Catholic missionaries. Formal congregations were few in 1790; itinerant ministers served scattered settlements.
- **Record types:** Baptism/christening registers, marriage registers, burial records. Confirmations were recorded by some denominations.
- **Where held:** Local denominational archives and the Ohio History Connection. FamilySearch has indexed 678,234 church records in 'Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950' (id: 2246917; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917). Digitization level: indexed + images for what has been microfilmed, but coverage of 1787-1800 is sparse.
- **Language:** English.
- **Gap warning:** Most itinerant ministers in 1790 did not keep systematic registers. Many early church records were never preserved. The absence of a church record for 1790 does not mean an event did not occur.

### Census records
- **Federal census 1790:** Ohio (Northwest Territory) is NOT enumerated in the 1790 federal census. Residents of the future state of Ohio will not appear there.
- **Federal census 1800:** The first enumeration to include Ohio, covering Washington and Hamilton counties. Head-of-household enumeration only — names only the head; other household members counted by age bracket.
- **Federal census 1810:** Ohio is enumerated as a state. Head-of-household enumeration.
- **No territorial or state census** for this period was identified in tool results.
- **Access:** 1800 and 1810 censuses are indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Territorial court records (1788-1803) include land grants, estate administrations, guardianships, and early civil cases. After 1803, the Court of Common Pleas took over probate jurisdiction.
- **Where held:** Early territorial records are at the Ohio History Connection, 800 E. 17th Ave., Columbus, OH 43211 (ohiohistory.org). Post-1803 probate is at the county courthouse.
- **Digitization:** No probate-specific volumes were returned by volume_search for the 1780-1810 window beyond the two volumes noted below. Likely physical or microfilm only for most 1790-era court material.

### Land records
- **Survey systems (three distinct and non-overlapping):**
  1. **United States Military Lands** (central Ohio): Federal rectangular survey; patents at BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov).
  2. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): Metes-and-bounds system using Virginia Revolutionary War bounty warrants. Records at the Virginia State Library and Archives, Richmond — not Ohio repositories.
  3. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio, present-day 14 counties): Township-grid survey; records at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840' (id: 1542187; 234,567 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187). Digitization level: indexed + images.
- **Digitized volumes:** volume_search returned one set of Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788-1799 (imageGroupNumber 005112233; 51 images; 0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable). This is browse-only — must be examined image by image with no search capability.
- **Critical quirk:** If your ancestor held land in the Virginia Military District, the land warrant and survey records are in Virginia, not Ohio. Search the Virginia State Library before concluding no land record exists.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (service records pre-date Ohio settlement but shaped who settled there via bounty land grants); Northwest Indian War / Little Turtle's War (1785-1795), including Harmar's Defeat (1790), St. Clair's Defeat (1791), and Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794).
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files at NARA (indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry); bounty land warrants; Northwest Indian War service records at NARA.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration, Washington D.C. / College Park, MD. Pension files are indexed and often partially digitized on Fold3 (fold3.com) and Ancestry.
- **Value:** Revolutionary War pension files (NARA) often contain autobiographical statements naming family members, migration routes, and dates — exceptionally valuable for 1790-era Ohio families.

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Settlement was sparse in 1790; formal cemeteries were rare. Family burial plots and early church graveyards are the norm.
- **Online:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves index tombstone inscriptions, but coverage of pre-1810 graves is very uneven.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for 1790 are virtually nonexistent given the settlement pattern.

### Newspaper records
- **Earliest Ohio newspaper:** The Centinel of the North-Western Territory, founded in Cincinnati in 1793 — the first newspaper in the Northwest Territory. No newspapers existed in Ohio in 1790.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) for later territorial-era papers.
- **Content value for 1790:** None directly; newspapers postdate the target year.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Migration routes:** Ohio settlers in 1790 arrived via: (a) the Ohio River from Pittsburgh, (b) overland from Virginia and Pennsylvania through southwestern Pennsylvania, (c) from New England via the Connecticut Western Reserve land company.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists are not relevant for this inland destination. Declarations of intention and naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — check territorial court records at the Ohio History Connection and early county court records.
- **Pennsylvania and Virginia origin records:** Because most 1790 Ohio settlers came from these states, searching Pennsylvania county deed and court records and Virginia county records is a necessary parallel track.

### Tax records
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850' (id: 1987542; 345,890 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542). The earliest year is 1800 — no tax records in this collection predate statehood.
- **Digitized volume:** One volume of Washington County Tax Records, 1799-1803 (imageGroupNumber 005112240; 73 images; 12% name-indexed; not full-text searchable). Partially searchable by name, but most entries require browsing.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1800 onward can place an individual in a county in off-census years.

### Other record types
- **Territorial administrative records:** Land patents, court minutes, and territorial governor's records are at the Ohio History Connection and NARA (Record Group 59, Territorial Papers of the United States, Ohio series).
- **BLM General Land Office:** Federal land patents for Ohio are searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov — the earliest Ohio patents date from the late 1780s.
- **NARA Territorial Papers:** The 'Territorial Papers of the United States' (M236 for the Northwest Territory) contain administrative correspondence that sometimes names individual settlers in land disputes, petitions, and complaints.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1.5M records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678K records); Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (235K records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (346K records); Northwest Territory Land Records 1788-1799 (browse-only images) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1800, 1810 for Ohio); Revolutionary War pension files | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records, pension files, Northwest Indian War records | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents for Ohio from late 1780s | Free |
| NARA / Fold3 | Territorial Papers of the United States (Northwest Territory, M236) | Free at NARA; subscription at Fold3 |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (very sparse pre-1810) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (none in Ohio before 1793) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Ohio in the 1780-1810 window — both are detailed above and the result set was complete (no nextPageToken). The FamilySearch collections figure (5 collections) is the complete set for Ohio in this period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial court records, state archives, county histories | In-person; some digitized at ohiohistory.org |
| NARA, Washington D.C. / College Park | Territorial Papers, military service/pension records | In-person; many records on Fold3/Ancestry |
| Virginia State Library and Archives, Richmond | Virginia Military District land warrants and surveys | In-person / mail request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve records | In-person |
| County courthouses | Post-1803 probate, deed, and court records | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Most territorial court minutes and case files (1788-1803) — held physically at the Ohio History Connection.
- Church registers from itinerant ministers serving 1787-1800 — scattered among denominational archives or lost.
- Virginia Military District survey plats and warrants — at Virginia State Library; not fully digitized.
- NARA Territorial Papers on microfilm (M236) — available at NARA reading rooms and some university libraries; not all digitized.

## Known record losses
- No specific courthouse fire or flood losses for the territorial period were identified in tool results for this survey window. However, the sparse settlement of 1790 means many events simply generated no written record at all — the absence of a record is often a documentation gap, not a record loss.
- Indigenous community records from this period are held in federal treaty records and Indian agent correspondence at NARA, not in Ohio state archives.

## Research tips
- **The 1790 census does not cover Ohio.** Residents of the Northwest Territory were not enumerated. The 1800 census is the earliest federal census source for Ohio families. [FamilySearch Wiki — Ohio Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory]
- **Determine the county before searching.** In 1790, only Washington County (east of the Scioto) and Hamilton County (west of the Scioto) existed. Later county formations after 1788 are irrelevant to a 1790 event. Work from a historical county boundary atlas — the Newberry Library's Atlas of Historical County Boundaries is the standard reference.
- **Land survey district determines which repository holds records.** Virginia Military District records go to Richmond, not Columbus. Connecticut Western Reserve records go to Cleveland. All other federal-land Ohio records go to BLM GLO online.
- **Revolutionary War pension files are a primary source.** Many Ohio settlers of 1790 were Revolutionary War veterans. Their pension applications at NARA often contain detailed life histories including where they moved and when. Search pension files at Fold3 or via NARA's pension index.
- **Church records substitute for absent civil registration.** Ohio had no civil vital registration in 1790. Seek baptism and marriage registers from Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Quaker records — and accept that no church record may exist if the family was served by itinerant ministers who kept no register.
- **Search the origin state in parallel.** Families arriving in Ohio in or before 1790 left records in Pennsylvania, Virginia, Kentucky, or New England before migrating. Those origin records may document family members not yet identifiable from Ohio sources.
- **NARA Territorial Papers (M236):** The Northwest Territory series contains land petitions, correspondence, and lists of settlers that occasionally name individuals not found elsewhere. Available on microfilm at NARA and major research libraries.

In 1790, the area we now call Ohio was still the Northwest Territory — a federally governed territory with only two organized counties in existence: Washington County (east of the Scioto River, formed 1788) and Hamilton County (west of it, formed 1790). Ohio did not become a state until 1803. That jurisdictional reality shapes everything about where records are held and what records even exist. There was no civil registration of births or deaths, no state government, and no newspapers. The primary records surviving from 1790 are land records (held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus, the Virginia State Library for the Military District, and the Western Reserve Historical Society for northeastern Ohio), early county marriage bonds beginning in 1789, Revolutionary War pension files at NARA (often the richest source for early settler life histories), and sparse church registers from itinerant ministers. Crucially, the 1790 federal census does not include Ohio at all — the first federal census covering Ohio is 1800. The two digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period are both browse-only or barely indexed, so most research requires either in-person visits to Columbus or NARA, or working from the few indexed online collections.

The next step is to build a research plan for your specific ancestor using this locality landscape as the foundation — beginning with the 1800 census, land records, and Revolutionary War pension files as the most productive starting points.

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Era), 1780-1810

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, covering present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. Ohio became the first state carved from it on 1 March 1803.
- **Administrative center:** Marietta (territorial capital); Columbus became the state capital in 1816.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory (federal), administered by the U.S. Congress under the Ordinance of 1787.
- **Population during period:** Population data returned no figures for this period from place_population — the region had very sparse Euro-American settlement in 1790. The 1800 federal census (the first to enumerate Ohio) counted approximately 45,000 residents in Washington and Hamilton counties.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, military garrison supply. The Ohio River was the primary migration and commerce corridor.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American settlers arriving from Virginia, Pennsylvania, New England, and Kentucky; significant Indigenous nations (Shawnee, Delaware/Lenape, Wyandot, Miami) whose own records are held separately in federal treaty and Indian agent records.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist itinerants, Presbyterian and Baptist missionaries were the earliest organized denominations. Quaker settlers arrived in the southeastern region. Catholic missionaries operated in some areas. Formal church structures were sparse in 1790.
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris 1783 opened the region to American settlement; Northwest Ordinance 1787 established governance; Battle of Fallen Timbers 1794 and Treaty of Greenville 1795 dramatically shifted the settler-Indigenous boundary and opened most of Ohio to settlement.

## Boundary changes
- **1787:** Northwest Ordinance creates the Northwest Territory — the entire future state of Ohio falls under this single territorial jurisdiction with no county subdivisions.
- **1788:** Washington County organized as the first county — covered all of present-day Ohio east of the Scioto River and south of Lake Erie.
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized — covered all of present-day Ohio west of the Scioto River.
- **1796 onward:** Additional counties carved rapidly from Washington and Hamilton counties as settlement expanded. Researchers must consult a boundary atlas to determine the correct county for any event before statehood.
- **1803:** Ohio achieves statehood. Records shift from territorial to state-level jurisdiction. Court of Common Pleas replaces territorial courts.
- **Key rule:** Any event in Ohio in 1790 was recorded (if at all) under Washington County or Hamilton County jurisdiction, depending on which side of the Scioto River the location falls. Never search a post-1803 county name for a 1790 event.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Ohio did not require civil registration of births and deaths at the statewide level until 1908. The FamilySearch Wiki specific Ohio Vital Records page did not return — generic content only was returned by that URL. No county-level civil registration date for the territorial period was found in tool results.
- **What exists for 1790:** No civil vital records exist for this period. Births, marriages, and deaths in 1790 were not registered by any government in the Northwest Territory.
- **Marriage records:** The FamilySearch collection 'Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013' (id: 1803785; 1,523,678 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) begins in 1789 and covers county-level marriage bonds and licenses. This is the earliest civil marriage record series available. Digitization level: indexed + images.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the only source for baptisms, marriages, and burials in 1790.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker (Society of Friends), and Catholic missionaries. Formal congregations were few in 1790; itinerant ministers served scattered settlements.
- **Record types:** Baptism/christening registers, marriage registers, burial records. Confirmations were recorded by some denominations.
- **Where held:** Local denominational archives and the Ohio History Connection. FamilySearch has indexed 678,234 church records in 'Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950' (id: 2246917; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917). Digitization level: indexed + images for what has been microfilmed, but coverage of 1787-1800 is sparse.
- **Language:** English.
- **Gap warning:** Most itinerant ministers in 1790 did not keep systematic registers. Many early church records were never preserved. The absence of a church record for 1790 does not mean an event did not occur.

### Census records
- **Federal census 1790:** Ohio (Northwest Territory) is NOT enumerated in the 1790 federal census. Residents of the future state of Ohio will not appear there.
- **Federal census 1800:** The first enumeration to include Ohio, covering Washington and Hamilton counties. Head-of-household enumeration only — names only the head; other household members counted by age bracket.
- **Federal census 1810:** Ohio is enumerated as a state. Head-of-household enumeration.
- **No territorial or state census** for this period was identified in tool results.
- **Access:** 1800 and 1810 censuses are indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Territorial court records (1788-1803) include land grants, estate administrations, guardianships, and early civil cases. After 1803, the Court of Common Pleas took over probate jurisdiction.
- **Where held:** Early territorial records are at the Ohio History Connection, 800 E. 17th Ave., Columbus, OH 43211 (ohiohistory.org). Post-1803 probate is at the county courthouse.
- **Digitization:** No probate-specific volumes were returned by volume_search for the 1780-1810 window beyond the two volumes noted below. Likely physical or microfilm only for most 1790-era court material.

### Land records
- **Survey systems (three distinct and non-overlapping):**
  1. **United States Military Lands** (central Ohio): Federal rectangular survey; patents at BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov).
  2. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): Metes-and-bounds system using Virginia Revolutionary War bounty warrants. Records at the Virginia State Library and Archives, Richmond — not Ohio repositories.
  3. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio, present-day 14 counties): Township-grid survey; records at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840' (id: 1542187; 234,567 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187). Digitization level: indexed + images.
- **Digitized volumes:** volume_search returned one set of Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788-1799 (imageGroupNumber 005112233; 51 images; 0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable). This is browse-only — must be examined image by image with no search capability.

### Cemetery records

- **Online:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves index tombstone inscriptions, but coverage of pre-1810 graves is very uneven.

### Newspaper records
- **Earliest Ohio newspaper:** The Centinel of the North-Western Territory, founded in Cincinnati in 1793 — the first newspaper in the Northwest Territory. No newspapers existed in Ohio in 1790.

- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1800 onward can place an individual in a county in off-census years.

- **Territorial administrative records:** Land patents, court minutes, and territorial governor's records are at the Ohio History Connection and NARA (Record Group 59, Territorial Papers of the United States, Ohio series).
- **BLM General Land Office:** Federal land patents for Ohio are searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov — the earliest Ohio patents date from the late 1780s.
- **NARA Territorial Papers:** The 'Territorial Papers of the United States' (M236 for the Northwest Territory) contain administrative correspondence that sometimes names individual settlers in land disputes, petitions, and complaints.

output.text_response:
Here's what the locality guide found for **California in the 1850s Gold Rush era**:

---

**Key starting points:**

- **1852 California State Census** (not 1850 federal — it's partially destroyed): 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch, making it the real anchor for that decade.
- **Passenger manifests**: For anyone who arrived by ship, indexed arrival records are on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Great Registers (from 1866)**: The richest name-indexed source for men who stayed — covers birthplace, occupation, and physical description.
- **County vital records (births/marriages from 1850)**: Indexed on FamilySearch. Death records for this period are thin; check newspapers, probate records, and mortality census schedules instead.

**Unindexed records that require page-by-page browsing:**
- Mining claim registers
- Port arrival registers

These are on FamilySearch but cannot be searched by name — you'll need to know the county or mining district first.

**Critical caveat — shifting county boundaries:** California county boundaries changed constantly in the 1850s. Always verify the correct county against a historical boundary map before running county-level searches.

**Top repository for serious research:**
The **Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley** holds diaries, letters, and primary sources from the Gold Rush era that no online database replicates. It's the essential archive for this period.

**Next step:** If you can narrow down the county or mining district your ancestor was in, a more targeted search plan becomes possible.

Mining Claim Registers (FamilySearch volume 006601002, 1849-1855) and Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento (volume 006601003, 1849-1858) are both 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — they must be browsed image by image.
Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — California county courts, California federal district courts, or eastern-state courts before migration. Search all three levels.

San Francisco city and county records created in the 1850s-1900s were largely destroyed in the 1906 earthquake and fire; FamilySearch microfilm and Bancroft Library copies are often the only surviving versions.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s — Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam founded by Dutch West India Company 1626; seized by England 1664 and renamed New York City.
- **Administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan), seat of New York County.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British Crown Colony) 1664–1776; New York State from 1777.
- **Population during period:** Tool returned no data. Estimated ~5,000 in 1700, ~33,000 by 1790 (first federal census).
- **Economy:** Maritime commerce, trade, and port activity; skilled trades; significant enslaved labor force.
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch-descended families, English settlers, Scots, French Huguenots, Sephardic Jewish merchants, West African enslaved people, Palatine Germans (esp. 1709-1710 wave).
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest, 1628), Anglican/Trinity Church (1697), Presbyterian (1716), French Reformed/Huguenot, Lutheran, Quaker, Congregation Shearith Israel (Jewish, 1654).
- **Key historical events:** British occupation during Revolutionary War (1776-1783); great fire of September 1776 destroyed ~25% of lower Manhattan.

## Boundary changes
- New York City was coterminous with New York County (Manhattan) throughout the 1700s.
- No mid-century splits of New York County occurred.
- Pre-1664 Dutch colonial records and post-1664 English records form one continuous research trail for Dutch-origin families.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration in New York City during the 1700s. Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1881 (state) and 1898 (NYC).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the only systematic vital record source.

### Church records
- Dutch Reformed: oldest continuous series, beginning 1639; 1 FamilySearch digitized volume (007733180, 211 images, 1700-1776, Dutch, 0% indexed, browse-only).
- Anglican/Trinity Church: registers from 1697; originals at Trinity Church Archives.
- Presbyterian (First Presbyterian, organized 1716): registers survive.
- French Reformed/Huguenot: registers in French.
- Lutheran: registers in German.
- Shearith Israel (Jewish): vital records published.
- FamilySearch collection 1469062 (New York, Church Records, 1640-1940) covers this period.

### Census records
- No federal census until 1790.
- Colonial enumerations: 1703, 1712, 1723, 1731, 1737, 1746, 1749, 1756 — head counts, not individual name lists; at New York State Archives.
- 1790 federal census indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- Colonial wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York (provincial level, not county).
- Indexed in Abstracts of Wills series (New-York Historical Society).
- FamilySearch collection 1542780 (New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971).
- Mayor's Court records at New York State Archives.

### Land records
- Royal patent and deed system; FamilySearch collection 2078654 (New York, Land Records, 1630-1975).
- New York Colonial Manuscripts at New York State Archives.

### Military records
- Colonial militia rolls at New York State Archives.
- Revolutionary War: NARA (service/pension records), Fold3 (subscription).

### Cemetery records
- Trinity Church burial ground; Shearith Israel cemetery (Chatham Square); African Burial Ground.
- FindAGrave covers Trinity headstones.

### Newspaper records
- New York Gazette (1725), New-York Weekly Journal (1733), New-York Mercury (1752).
- Partial coverage: Newspapers.com (subscription), Chronicling America (free, Library of Congress).

### Immigration/emigration records
- Pre-1820 passenger lists are fragmentary; no systematic government manifests.
- Palatine German wave of 1709-1710 has published specialized indexes.
- NARA for post-1790 naturalizations.

### Tax records
- Ward-based tax assessment lists survive for some years; serve as census substitute.
- FamilySearch collection 1678432 covers 1799-1804 only.
- Earlier ward tax lists at NYC Municipal Archives and New York State Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collections 1469062, 2078654, 1542780, 1678432 | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 federal census; additional NY colonial records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension/muster rolls | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Some colonial NY newspapers | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Some colonial NY newspapers | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military and naturalization records | Free/in-person |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | Colonial Manuscripts; Prerogative Court probate; colonial censuses; militia rolls | In-person; finding aids at archives.nysed.gov |
| NYC Municipal Archives | City administrative records; later vital records | In-person or written request |
| New-York Historical Society | Abstracts of Wills series; manuscript collections; newspaper microfilm | In-person by appointment |
| NYGBS (New York) | Colonial church register transcriptions; NYGB Record | In-person; some digital for members |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican registers from 1697 | Contact directly |
| Reformed Church in America Archives (NJ) | Dutch Reformed registers | In-person or written request |
| Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia) | Presbyterian church records | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Ward tax lists predating 1799.
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (provincial administrative records).
- Colonial militia rolls.
- Mayor's Court colonial-era records.
- Most church registers beyond the Dutch Reformed FamilySearch volume.
- French Huguenot and German Lutheran registers.

## Known record losses
- Great fire of September 1776 destroyed ~25% of lower Manhattan; some municipal records lost.
- British occupation (1776-1783) disrupted local government records; some records now at The National Archives (UK, Kew).
- Some pre-1664 Dutch records damaged or incomplete.

## Research tips
- Church records are your vital records — there is no civil registration for the 1700s.
- Dutch Reformed registers are browse-only and in Dutch; use published transcriptions or a translator.
- Probate records went to the Prerogative Court, not the county — start with the Abstracts of Wills series.
- Use ward tax lists and militia rolls as census substitutes before 1790.
- The NYGB Record (published since 1870) is essential for colonial New York research.
- Search neighboring counties (Kings, Queens, Westchester, Richmond) for family members.
- Dutch families used patronymic surnames into the early 1700s — allow for surname variation.
- For German-background families arriving around 1709-1710, use the specialized Palatine emigration indexes.
- British occupation records (1776-1783) may be at The National Archives (UK, Kew).

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** Virginia was the largest and most populous of the thirteen colonies, fighting as a founding state from the war's outbreak in 1775 through the decisive Siege of Yorktown in October 1781, with hostilities ending in 1783.
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital); Richmond became the capital in 1780.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Virginia under the British Crown until 1776; thereafter the Commonwealth of Virginia.
- **Population during period:** No tool result returned population figures for this exact window. Wikipedia confirms Virginia was the most populous colony and contributed more Continental Army troops than any other state.
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation agriculture in the Tidewater and Piedmont; mixed farming and frontier settlement in the Valley and western counties; some iron manufacturing.
- **Ethnic composition:** English-descended settlers dominant; Scots-Irish and German settlers concentrated in the Shenandoah Valley; substantial enslaved African American population; small numbers of free Black Virginians.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal; Presbyterian; Baptist; Methodist; Lutheran and German Reformed (Valley and Piedmont).
- **Key historical events:** Virginia Provincial Convention (1775); Declaration of Independence (1776); British invasion of the Tidewater (1781); Siege of Yorktown (October 1781); Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty program launched post-war.

## Boundary changes
Virginia's boundaries during 1775–1783 were broadly stable within the state proper, but the western counties were expanding rapidly. Kentucky County was formed from Fincastle County in 1776, then partitioned (Lincoln, Jefferson, Fayette counties) in 1780. If your ancestor was in far western Virginia, identify the exact county and its formation date; records before formation are held by the parent county. The 1782 personal property tax list is the earliest statewide enumeration and was created because Virginia's 1790 federal census was later destroyed.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page did not return Virginia-specific content in this session.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses recorded at the county level by the county clerk.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900; ~2.5 million records, name-indexed, images online).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary substitute.

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, German Reformed.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; Anglican vestry books (tithe lists, poor relief, orphan binding).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929; ~1.2 million records, name-indexed, images online). Originals at diocesan archives and county courthouses.
- **Language:** English for Anglican/Episcopal and most Baptist records; German for Lutheran and Reformed records in the Valley.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 returns for Virginia were destroyed in 1814. No federal census exists for 1775–1783.
- **State enumerations / tax lists:** 1782 and 1783 personal property tax lists are the standard substitute. Volume 005301449 (87 images, full-text searchable, not name-indexed) covers 1782–1799. FamilySearch collection 1456723 (Tax Records, 1782–1850; ~456,000 records, name-indexed, images online).

### Military records
- **Continental Army:** CMSR files at NARA (RG 93); FamilySearch collection 1945678 (Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783; ~345,000 records, name-indexed, images online).
- **Virginia militia:** Muster rolls, pay vouchers, and order books at the Library of Virginia; not fully digitized.
- **Pension and bounty land warrants:** NARA RG 15; Fold3 (subscription). Virginia's own bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio are at the Library of Virginia.
- **Digitized volumes:** Volume 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800, 341 images, browse-only — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship bonds, county court order books.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2134567 (Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920; ~1.7 million records, name-indexed, images online). Augusta County court order books also available as volume 005301448 (158 images, 61% name-indexed).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (state-land state).
- **Types:** Colonial land patents, county deed books, surveys, tax records, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900). Originals at county courthouses and Library of Virginia.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax, land tax.
- **Date range:** Annual lists begin 1782.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 (Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850; name-indexed, images online); volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, 87 images, browse-only).

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves (partial coverage for this period).
- **Physical records:** Vestry books record some Anglican burials; sexton records not systematically kept.

### Military/wartime-specific records
- **Virginia Gazette deserter notices:** Name soldiers and give physical descriptions.
- **Confiscated Loyalist estate sales:** County court and newspaper records.
- **British Loyalist Claims Commission:** Files at The National Archives, Kew, UK, for Loyalists who fled Virginia.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** Transatlantic immigration was nearly halted by the war. Post-war migration out of Virginia (to Kentucky, Tennessee, Ohio) begins 1781–1783.
- **Sources:** County deed books (land sold before departure), bounty land warrants (record state of origin), British Loyalist Claims Commission records (Kew, UK).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 5 collections covering military, church, land/marriage/will, tax, and county court records | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War CMSR, pension application files | Subscription |
| Ancestry.com | NARA pension files index, colonial Virginia records, post-1800 census | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | RG 93 (service records), RG 15 (pensions/bounty land) | Free finding aids; files on Fold3/Ancestry |
| Newspapers.com / GenealogyBank | Virginia Gazette and successor papers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |

**Coverage note:** Volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes total (all detailed above); this is the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia (Richmond) | Militia records, land grants/patents, bounty land warrants, county deed books, tax lists | In-person; some online at lva.virginia.gov |
| National Archives (Washington, D.C.) | CMSR (RG 93), pension/bounty land files (RG 15) | In-person; many on Fold3/Ancestry |
| County courthouses | Original deed books, will books, order books, marriage bonds | In-person or county clerk by mail |
| Virginia Museum of History & Culture | Published county histories, manuscript collections, diaries | In-person (Richmond) |
| Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives | Anglican/Episcopal parish registers and vestry books | In-person or written request |
| Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia) | Virginia Presbyterian session books | In-person or written request |
| The National Archives, Kew, UK | British Loyalist Claims Commission files for Virginia Loyalists | In-person or online (Discovery catalogue) |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia muster rolls and pay vouchers (most at Library of Virginia; not systematically digitized)
- Anglican vestry books (some microfilmed; most originals at county courthouses or diocesan archives)
- British Loyalist Claims Commission files (Kew, UK)
- Most local newspaper microfilm beyond partial digital coverage

## Known record losses
- **Virginia's 1790 federal census:** Destroyed 1814. Use 1782–1783 tax lists as substitute.
- **County courthouse fires:** Hanover, James City, and other counties suffered fires destroying some deed and will books. Check whether your county has known losses.
- **Anglican parish register gaps:** Disestablishment after 1776 interrupted register-keeping in many parishes.

## Research tips
- Start with the pension file (NARA RG 15, Fold3) — richest single document for Revolutionary War veterans.
- Use the 1782 personal property tax list as the census substitute for the lost 1790 Virginia returns.
- Search both Continental CMSR files and Virginia militia records — service in both was common.
- Virginia bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio (Library of Virginia, volume 005301447) connect veterans to post-war migration.
- County court order books name militia exemptions, supply contractors, and estate settlements — people who never appear in service records.
- Anglican vestry books list every taxable household annually and record poor relief and orphan binding — a near-census for 1775–1783.
- Kentucky was Virginia jurisdiction 1776–1792 — search Virginia-era county records held in Kentucky courthouses.
- Valley Lutheran/German Reformed records are in German script — plan for translation if researching Augusta, Rockingham, Shenandoah, or Frederick counties.

Here is the locality guide's full response on New Orleans early-1800s records, disaster losses, and where to find substitutes:

---

## What Survived — and What Didn't

**The two fires are the central fact.** The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of French Quarter colonial civil records before 1800. Recurring floods and yellow fever epidemics continued to cause losses throughout the early 1800s. You should assume gaps in pre-1800 originals and expect gaps within 1800–1860 as well.

**What survived best:**

1. **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps). These are the primary substitute for missing civil vital records. FamilySearch collection 1612905 (*Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925*) has indexed images. Many records through the 1820s are in French or Spanish.

2. **Notarial records** — Louisiana's civil law (Napoleonic Code) tradition routed sales, contracts, successions, emancipations, property transfers, and many life events through professional notaries who kept multiple office copies. The fires hit them less hard than administrative records. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds 30+ million pages dating to 1734. Only a small 167-image microfilm sample (1803–1820) is on FamilySearch — the bulk requires in-person or research-request access.

3. **Succession (probate) records** — FamilySearch collection 2078341 (*Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984*). Note the vocabulary: Louisiana uses "successions" not "probate," "tutorships" not "guardianships."

4. **Cabildo records** (Spanish colonial) — survived in part at the Louisiana State Museum.

---

## Where to Look for Copies or Substitutes

| When originals are missing | Look here instead |
|---|---|
| Civil vital records | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (FamilySearch coll. 1612905) |
| Court/deed records | Notarial acts (Notarial Archives Research Center; partial FamilySearch browse vol. 004990115) |
| Proof of family relationships | Louisiana successions (FamilySearch coll. 2078341) |
| Non-household-head tracking between censuses | Tax rolls (Louisiana State Archives); notarial acts |
| Immigration/arrival | Passenger lists at Ancestry.com / NARA; Port of New Orleans was a major entry point |
| Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices | New Orleans newspapers — *The Bee*, *Daily Picayune* (Newspapers.com; Tulane microfilm) |
| Enslaved and free-Black ancestors | Louisiana Slave Database; FreedomOnTheMove.org; notarial manumission acts; sacramental registers |

---

## Key Practical Warnings

- **Language barrier:** Many records through at least the 1820s are in French or Spanish — plan for translation.
- **Vocabulary barrier:** Use "successions," "tutorships," and "notarial acts" — not "probate," "guardianship," or "deeds" — or you'll miss records entirely.
- **Most of the notarial archive is not online.** The 30+ million pages at the Notarial Archives Research Center require in-person or written-request access. FamilySearch has only one 167-image microfilm sample.
- **Before 1850, federal censuses name only the head of household.** Use tax rolls and notarial acts to trace other family members between census years.

The guide has been saved to the project as `loc_001`. The recommended next step is a research plan routing searches through the St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers and the notarial archives first, for any ancestor in this period.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by France; passed to Spain 1763; briefly returned to France; acquired by the United States via the Louisiana Purchase 1803. The Territory of Orleans was organized 1804; Louisiana became a state 1812, at which point Orleans Parish was constituted as the parish coextensive with the city.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish are effectively the same jurisdiction for this period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804–1812), then State of Louisiana (1812–)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this place and period. Wikipedia notes the city grew rapidly through immigration from France, Spain, Africa, Saint-Domingue (Haiti), and later Ireland and Germany across the early-to-mid 1800s.
- **Economy:** Major Mississippi River port, cotton and sugar trade, river commerce, enslaved labor economy
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, free people of color, enslaved Africans, Haitian refugees (post-1804), Irish immigrants, German immigrants, Anglo-American migrants
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral the central parish), Protestant denominations arrived with Anglo-American migration post-1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); fires of 1788 and 1794 (destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial records); repeated yellow fever epidemics throughout the period; Battle of New Orleans (1815); steady waves of immigration throughout

## Boundary changes
- Stable at the parish level from 1812 onward for this period.
- Before 1812, records were created under the Territory of Orleans and, before 1804, under Spanish colonial and briefly French colonial government. Records from those regimes follow their own archival trails (see Church Records and Notarial Records below).
- No split or subdivision of Orleans Parish occurred in this period.

## Known record losses

This is the most critical section for New Orleans early 1800s research.

**Fires of 1788 and 1794:** Two catastrophic fires destroyed most of the French Quarter and a substantial portion of the colonial-era built record environment. Many pre-1800 civil and administrative documents did not survive. Researchers should assume gaps in pre-1800 originals and work from transcriptions, microfilm copies, and duplicate series.

**Yellow fever epidemics and flooding:** Repeated epidemics and hurricane flooding throughout the early 1800s caused additional damage to archival holdings at multiple repositories. Gaps in surviving record series should be expected across the 1800–1860 window, not just at the colonial boundary.

**Substitute and survival strategies:**
- Sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) are the primary substitute for missing civil vital records.
- Notarial records are exceptionally rich and survived comparatively well — they were maintained by professional notaries whose offices often preserved multiple copies. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages dating to 1734 ([New Orleans Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)).
- Louisiana succession (probate) records at FamilySearch (collection 2078341, 1756–1984) may document family relationships when vital records are absent.
- The Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body) survived in part and are held at the Louisiana State Museum.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey — the exact registration-start date and level cannot be confirmed from tool results. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists:** Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892; index only, no images; 2,345,678 records) overlaps this period from 1819.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps due to disaster losses); notarial records documenting births and deaths incidentally.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant — St. Louis Cathedral), with Protestant churches established after 1803 Anglo-American migration.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (sacramental registers). Confirmations are a separate dated event and appear in separate series.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral archives; FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925; 987,654 records, 493,827 images — indexed + images).
- **Language:** Records are frequently in French or Spanish, especially before about 1820. Researchers must be able to read the original language or use a translation aid.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (collection 1612905 on FamilySearch)
- **Gaps:** Fire losses mean pre-1800 series have gaps; post-fire transcription efforts partially compensate.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860 decennial censuses cover this period. The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses predate Louisiana statehood and territorial organization, so coverage is limited or absent for New Orleans specifically.
- **State/territorial census:** The FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana Census page returned only generic content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Census for any state/territorial enumeration dates.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for Louisiana are widely available on Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). 1850 and 1860 include individual names, ages, birthplaces, and occupations; earlier censuses are head-of-household only.

### Probate and court records (successions and tutorships)
- **Types:** Louisiana uses civil-law succession records rather than common-law probate. Search for 'successions' (estates) and 'tutorships' (guardianship), not just 'wills' and 'administrations.' Interdictions (incompetency proceedings) are also unique to Louisiana civil law.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984; 456,789 records, 228,394 images) covers this period.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); FamilySearch collection 2078341.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (collection 2078341 on FamilySearch)

### Notarial records
- **Unique to Louisiana:** Under Louisiana's civil law (Napoleonic Code) tradition, professional notaries recorded sales, contracts, successions, emancipations, and many life events that common-law states routed through courts or left unrecorded.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages, dating to 1734). FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115): 167 images of surviving microfilm copies of notarial acts, 1803–1820, bilingual French/English, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image-by-image.
- **Access level:** Browse-only images (FamilySearch); physical and in-person access at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for the broader collection.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses a French/Spanish metes-and-bounds system with arpent measurements — distinct from the federal township-and-range system used in most U.S. states.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana Land and Property page returned only generic content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property for which office holds grants and patents.
- **Types:** Notarial deeds, Spanish land grants, American-era land patents, tax records. Land sales and transfers are often recorded in notarial acts rather than a county deed book.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Land Office; New Orleans Notarial Archives; Louisiana State Archives.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, 1815); Mexican-American War (1846–1848)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft/muster rolls at NARA (fold3.com, archives.gov). Louisiana militia records may be at the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C.); Fold3 (subscription); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (founded 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (founded 1823), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (founded 1833) — New Orleans's above-ground tomb tradition.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for New Orleans cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at the Archdiocese of New Orleans archives and individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New Orleans Bee (L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans, bilingual French/English, founded 1827); the Louisiana Gazette; the Times-Picayune (founded 1837 as the Daily Picayune)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription, https://www.newspapers.com/); Louisiana State Library microfilm holdings; Tulane University Special Collections.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, sheriff's sale notices, runaway slave advertisements, legal notices, ship arrival lists.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New Orleans was one of the busiest in the United States; a major entry point for French, Spanish, Haitian, Irish, and German immigrants.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA; Ancestry.com); naturalization declarations filed in local courts (pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record); border crossing records.
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Ancestry.com (subscription); Fold3 (subscription).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Louisiana levied property tax and poll tax; Orleans Parish assessment rolls document property ownership.
- **Date range:** Assessment rolls survive from the territorial period onward with gaps.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); Orleans Parish archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls are especially valuable as a substitute for pre-1850 census years when only heads of household were enumerated, and as a year-by-year presence check between census years.

### Other record types
- **Slave records:** Louisiana has some of the most extensive documentary records of enslaved persons in North America, recorded in sacramental registers, notarial acts (sales, emancipations, manumissions), and succession inventories. FreedomOnTheMove.org and the Louisiana Slave Database are specialized resources.
- **Free people of color:** New Orleans had one of the largest and most legally distinct free Black communities in the antebellum United States. Their records appear in church registers, notarial acts, and court records in a partially separate administrative track.
- **Spanish colonial records (Cabildo):** Administrative records of the Spanish governing body survive in part at the Louisiana State Museum (the Cabildo building) and the Louisiana State Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana Church Records 1718–1925 (1612905); Louisiana Parish Marriages 1837–1957 (1798054); Louisiana Probate Records 1756–1984 (2078341); Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819–1964 (1543892); Notarial Acts 1803–1820 browse-only volume (004990115) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census collection (all decades 1810–1860); passenger arrival lists; additional Louisiana collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records for New Orleans cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, passenger lists, naturalization | Free/request |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch collections_search returned 4 indexed collections at the Louisiana state level. volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Orleans Parish (1803–1820 notarial acts, 167 images, browse-only). The external_links_search returned 6 curated third-party links (generic-level, not New Orleans-specific). The wiki_place_page tool returned only generic content for all four Louisiana sections — no Louisiana-specific wiki page text was retrieved.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; research requests |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state records; succession records; tax rolls; militia records | In-person; online catalog |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers; burial records | In-person; written request |
| Louisiana State Museum (The Cabildo) | Spanish colonial Cabildo records | In-person |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Newspapers; local history; Afro-Louisiana records | In-person |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Court records; succession files | In-person / clerk request |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta, GA) | Federal records for Louisiana | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online
- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives (30+ million pages) exists physically at the Research Center; only a 167-image microfilm sample (1803–1820) is on FamilySearch.
- Orleans Parish civil and court records that predate digitization remain on paper or microfilm at the courthouse and Louisiana State Archives.
- Spanish colonial Cabildo records are primarily held physically at the Louisiana State Museum.
- Archdiocese sacramental registers earlier than those captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905 may exist only in the Archdiocese archives.
- Cemetery sexton records and burial registers are primarily held at the individual cemeteries and the Archdiocese.

## Known record losses
- **Fire of 1788:** Destroyed a large portion of the French Quarter and many colonial civil records.
- **Fire of 1794:** A second catastrophic fire caused further destruction of records and the built environment.
- **Yellow fever epidemics (recurring, especially 1817, 1819, 1822, 1832, 1853):** Overwhelmed record-keeping capacity and damaged storage conditions for existing records.
- **Hurricane and flood damage (recurring):** Repeated flooding damaged repositories throughout the period.
- **Substitute sources:** Notarial records (multiple copies, professionally maintained), St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (partially transcribed and microfilmed), and succession/court records often preserve information lost from civil vital records.

## Research tips
- New Orleans suffered catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794; the New Orleans Genealogy wiki search result specifically identifies St. Louis Cathedral registers, notarial records, and Cabildo records as the main survivors ([New Orleans Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)).
- Louisiana's civil law system means legal records are organized around notarial acts and successions, not the common-law deed books and probate courts familiar to researchers from other U.S. states. Adjust search vocabulary accordingly.
- Many records through at least the 1820s are in French or Spanish. Plan for language work or hire a translator familiar with period notarial and ecclesiastical handwriting.
- Before 1850, federal censuses name only the head of household. Use tax rolls and notarial acts to track non-household-heads between census years.
- New Orleans was a major port of entry. Passenger arrival lists at Ancestry.com and NARA are essential for tracing immigrant ancestors — the full manifest lists all family members, including infants.
- For enslaved and free-Black ancestors, the sacramental registers, notarial manumission acts, and the Louisiana Slave Database / FreedomOnTheMove.org are starting points not found in standard vital record searches.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's hosted pages for Louisiana (all four research sections and all targeted topic pages) returned only generic content in this survey — check the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for current, Louisiana-specific guidance.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by France in 1718, transferred to Spain in 1763, briefly returned to France, then acquired by the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. The Territory of Orleans was organized in 1804; Louisiana became a state in 1812, at which point Orleans Parish was constituted as the civil parish coextensive with the city.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish are the same jurisdiction for this period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804–1812), then State of Louisiana (1812–)
- **Population during period:** No figures were returned by the population tool for this place and period. Wikipedia notes the city grew rapidly through French, Spanish, African, Haitian, Irish, and German immigration across the early-to-mid 1800s.
- **Economy:** Major Mississippi River port; cotton and sugar trade; river commerce; enslaved labor economy
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, free people of color, enslaved Africans, Haitian refugees (post-1804), Irish immigrants, German immigrants, Anglo-American migrants
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral the central parish); Protestant denominations arrived with Anglo-American migration after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); fires of 1788 and 1794; recurring yellow fever epidemics; Battle of New Orleans (1815); sustained waves of immigration

## Boundary changes
- Stable at the parish level from 1812 onward within this period.
- Before 1812, records were created under the Territory of Orleans and, before 1804, under Spanish colonial and briefly French colonial government. Those regimes follow their own archival trails (see Church Records and Notarial Records below).
- No subdivision of Orleans Parish occurred in this period.

## Known record losses

This is the most critical section for New Orleans early-1800s research.

**Fire of 1788:** Destroyed a large portion of the French Quarter and many colonial civil records.

**Fire of 1794:** A second catastrophic fire caused further destruction of records and the built environment.

**Yellow fever epidemics (recurring — especially 1817, 1819, 1822, 1832, 1853):** Overwhelmed record-keeping capacity and damaged storage conditions for existing records.

**Hurricane and flood damage (recurring throughout the period):** Repeated flooding damaged repositories.

**What this means for researchers:** Assume gaps in pre-1800 originals and expect gaps within the 1800–1860 window as well. The fires of 1788 and 1794 are directly named in the [New Orleans Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) as the cause of major record loss, and that page identifies the main survivors: sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral, notarial records, and Cabildo records.

**Substitute and survival strategies:**
- Sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) are the primary substitute for missing civil vital records.
- Notarial records survived comparatively well because professional notaries maintained multiple copies in their offices. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages dating to 1734.
- Louisiana succession records (FamilySearch collection 2078341, 1756–1984) document family relationships when vital records are absent.
- Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body) survived in part and are held at the Louisiana State Museum.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey — the exact registration-start date and the level at which it applied (parish vs. statewide) could not be confirmed from tool results. Check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records directly before assuming civil records exist for any given year in this period.
- **What exists (confirmed from tools):** Louisiana Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892; index only, no images; 2,345,678 entries). This overlaps the period from 1819 onward but provides no images.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; notarial acts that document births and deaths incidentally.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant — St. Louis Cathedral), with Protestant churches established after 1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Confirmations are a separate dated event and appear in their own series.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral archives; FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925; ~987,654 records, ~493,827 images).
- **Language:** Many records through at least the 1820s are in French or Spanish. Researchers must read the original language or use a specialized translation aid.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
- **Gaps:** Fire losses mean pre-1800 series have gaps; some post-fire transcription efforts partially compensate.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860 decennial censuses cover this period. Before 1850, only heads of household are named.
- **State/territorial census:** The FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana Census page returned only generic content — check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Census for any state or territorial enumeration dates.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for Louisiana are widely available on Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free).

### Probate and court records (successions and tutorships)
- **Types:** Louisiana uses civil-law succession records, not common-law probate. Search for "successions" (estates) and "tutorships" (guardianship), and also "interdictions" (incompetency proceedings) — not just "wills" and "administrations."

- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); FamilySearch collection 2078341 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341).
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch)

### Notarial records (unique to Louisiana)
- **Why they matter:** Under Louisiana's civil law (Napoleonic Code) tradition, professional notaries recorded sales, contracts, successions, emancipations, property transfers, and many life events that common-law states routed through courts or left undocumented. ### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, 1815); Mexican-American War (1846–1848)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft and muster rolls at NARA; Louisiana militia records at the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Fold3 (subscription, https://www.fold3.com/); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (founded 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (founded 1823), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (founded 1833) — New Orleans's above-ground tomb tradition.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for New Orleans cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at the Archdiocese of New Orleans archives and individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New Orleans Bee (L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans, bilingual French/English, founded 1827); the Louisiana Gazette; the Daily Picayune (founded 1837).
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription, https://www.newspapers.com/); Louisiana State Library microfilm; Tulane University Special Collections.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, sheriff's sale notices, runaway slave advertisements, legal notices, ship arrival lists — many events that were never entered into civil registers.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** The Port of New Orleans was one of the busiest in the United States and a primary entry point for French, Spanish, Haitian, Irish, and German immigrants.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA and Ancestry.com; naturalization declarations filed in local courts (pre-1906, any court of record).
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Ancestry.com (subscription); Fold3 (subscription).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and poll tax; Orleans Parish assessment rolls document property ownership year by year.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); Orleans Parish archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls are especially valuable for tracking non-household-heads between census years, and as a presence check in years between federal censuses.

### Other record types
- **Slave records:** Louisiana has some of the most extensive documentary records of enslaved persons in North America, recorded in sacramental registers, notarial acts (sales, emancipations, manumissions), and succession inventories. FreedomOnTheMove.org and the Louisiana Slave Database are specialized resources.
- **Free people of color:** New Orleans had one of the largest and most legally distinct free Black communities in the antebellum United States. Their records appear in church registers, notarial acts, and court records — sometimes in a partially separate administrative track requiring targeted searching.
- **Spanish colonial Cabildo records:** Administrative records of the Spanish governing body survive in part at the Louisiana State Museum (the Cabildo building) and the Louisiana State Archives.

- Archdiocese sacramental registers earlier than those captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905 may exist only in the Archdiocese archives.
- Cemetery sexton records and burial registers are primarily held at the individual cemeteries and the Archdiocese.

## Known record losses
- **Fire of 1788:** Destroyed a large portion of the French Quarter and many colonial civil records.
- **Fire of 1794:** A second catastrophic fire caused further destruction of records and the built environment.
- **Yellow fever epidemics (recurring, especially 1817, 1819, 1822, 1832, 1853):** Overwhelmed record-keeping capacity and damaged storage conditions for existing records.
- **Hurricane and flood damage (recurring):** Repeated flooding damaged repositories throughout the period.
- **Substitute sources:** Notarial records (multiple copies, professionally maintained), St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (partially transcribed and microfilmed), and succession/court records often preserve information lost from civil vital records.

- New Orleans suffered catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794; the New Orleans Genealogy wiki search result specifically identifies St. Louis Cathedral registers, notarial records, and Cabildo records as the main survivors ([New Orleans Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)).
