entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood Period, 1760–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** Not a colony; the territory was contested between New Hampshire and New York. After 1777 it existed as the independent Republic of Vermont until admission as the 14th U.S. state on March 4, 1791.
- **Predecessor claims:** New Hampshire issued land grants ("New Hampshire Grants") from 1749. New York asserted competing jurisdiction from 1764 and issued its own patents. Neither colony governed the territory effectively on the ground.
- **Administrative center:** No single colonial capital; the Republic of Vermont operated with its legislature moving between towns.
- **Parent jurisdictions for records:** Town governments (under the Republic of Vermont) for most civil records. Federal records begin with statehood in 1791.
- **Population during period:** No tool-returned population figure is available for this exact period. The first federal census (1790) counted Vermont after statehood; Vermont's recorded 1791 population was approximately 85,000.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, small-scale grain and timber production, potash export. Settlement was largely frontier and scattered.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descent New Englanders migrating north and west from Massachusetts and Connecticut; smaller numbers from New Hampshire and New York.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Presbyterian, Quaker, and Methodist congregations beginning to form in the 1780s. The Church of England was not established here.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (ending 1763) opened the territory to settlement; the Green Mountain Boys resisted New York authority from the 1760s; Revolutionary War service 1775–1783; Vermont Constitution of 1777 (the first in North America to prohibit adult slavery); statehood 1791.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1764, the territory was administered by New Hampshire (Governor Benning Wentworth issued grants). After 1764 the Privy Council placed the Connecticut River as New York's eastern boundary, assigning the Grants area to New York — but settlers holding New Hampshire patents refused to comply.
- Vermont declared independence in 1777 and operated as a republic with its own land office and court system.
- At statehood (1791), Vermont's boundaries were essentially those of the present state. No subsequent boundary changes are relevant to this period.
- **Research implication:** A land record from the 1760s–1770s may exist as a New Hampshire grant, a New York patent, a Vermont Republic re-grant, or all three for the same parcel. Search all three sources.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in 1857 — well after the pre-statehood period. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Vermont states: "Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857." (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Earlier town clerk records:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that "Earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly." These are not a uniform statewide series — each town's survival is independent.
- **What exists for 1760–1791:** Sporadic town clerk entries of births, marriages, and deaths in town meeting books and proprietors' records, beginning in the 1770s for established towns. No centralized pre-statehood vital registration existed.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices in each Vermont town; some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch or transcribed by local historical societies.
- **Gaps:** Most early vital events in this period are simply not in any civil record. Church registers and family bibles are the primary substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers; family Bible records; gravestone inscriptions; town meeting books that incidentally record vital events.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist churches were established in many Vermont towns as settlement began (1760s–1780s). Baptist and Methodist congregations formed in the 1780s. Quaker meetings existed in some communities.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (christenings), marriages, burials, membership lists, and in some congregations, confession-of-faith records. Confirmations were not a standard feature of Congregationalist or Baptist practice, so they are not a separate dated event series here.
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Where held:** Records of surviving congregations may be at the local church, at denominational archives (Congregationalist records often at the Congregational Library in Boston; Baptist records with the American Baptist Historical Society), or microfilmed by FamilySearch. The FamilySearch topic-specific Vermont Church Records page did not return Vermont-specific content at the time of this survey — consult FamilySearch.org directly.
- **Access:** Varies. Some have been transcribed by the Vermont Historical Society or county genealogical societies. Physical-only for many.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal decennial census was taken in 1790. Vermont appears in the 1790 census (taken after its March 1791 admission) — this is the earliest national enumeration for Vermont. It lists heads of household by name with counts of free white males, females, and other persons; it does not name individuals other than heads of household.
- **Pre-statehood enumerations:** No Vermont-specific census was conducted during the Republic of Vermont period. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Vermont Census did not return Vermont-specific content at the time of this survey.
- **Tax lists as census substitutes:** Vermont towns conducted tax assessments; these lists name property-holding residents and are critical substitutes for missing census coverage before 1790.

- **Administrative center:** No single colonial capital; the Republic of Vermont's legislature moved between towns.

- **Population during period:** No tool-returned population figure is available for this exact period. The 1790 federal census recorded Vermont's population at approximately 85,000 shortly after statehood.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, small-scale grain and timber production, potash export. Settlement was largely frontier and scattered.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descent New Englanders migrating north and west from Massachusetts and Connecticut; smaller numbers from New Hampshire and New York.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Presbyterian, Quaker, and Methodist congregations beginning to form in the 1780s. The Church of England was not established here.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood Period, 1760–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** Not a colony; the territory was contested between New Hampshire and New York. After 1777 it existed as the independent Republic of Vermont until admission as the 14th U.S. state on March 4, 1791.
- **Predecessor claims:** New Hampshire issued land grants ("New Hampshire Grants") from 1749. New York asserted competing jurisdiction from 1764 and issued its own patents. Neither colony governed the territory effectively on the ground.
- **Administrative center:** No single colonial capital; the Republic of Vermont operated with its legislature moving between towns.
- **Parent jurisdictions for records:** Town governments (under the Republic of Vermont) for most civil records. Federal records begin with statehood in 1791.
- **Population during period:** No tool-returned population figure is available for this exact period. The first federal census (1790) counted Vermont after statehood; Vermont's recorded 1791 population was approximately 85,000.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, small-scale grain and timber production, potash export. Settlement was largely frontier and scattered.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descent New Englanders migrating north and west from Massachusetts and Connecticut; smaller numbers from New Hampshire and New York.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Presbyterian, Quaker, and Methodist congregations beginning to form in the 1780s. The Church of England was not established here.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (ending 1763) opened the territory to settlement; the Green Mountain Boys resisted New York authority from the 1760s; Revolutionary War service 1775–1783; Vermont Constitution of 1777 (the first in North America to prohibit adult slavery); statehood 1791.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1764, the territory was administered by New Hampshire (Governor Benning Wentworth issued grants). After 1764 the Privy Council placed the Connecticut River as New York's eastern boundary, assigning the Grants area to New York — but settlers holding New Hampshire patents refused to comply.
- Vermont declared independence in 1777 and operated as a republic with its own land office and court system.
- At statehood (1791), Vermont's boundaries were essentially those of the present state. No subsequent boundary changes are relevant to this period.
- **Research implication:** A land record from the 1760s–1770s may exist as a New Hampshire grant, a New York patent, a Vermont Republic re-grant, or all three for the same parcel. Search all three sources.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in 1857 — well after the pre-statehood period. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Vermont states: "Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857." (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Earlier town clerk records:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that "Earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly." These are not a uniform statewide series — each town's survival is independent.
- **What exists for 1760–1791:** Sporadic town clerk entries of births, marriages, and deaths in town meeting books and proprietors' records, beginning in the 1770s for established towns. No centralized pre-statehood vital registration existed.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices in each Vermont town; some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch or transcribed by local historical societies.
- **Gaps:** Most early vital events in this period are simply not in any civil record. Church registers and family bibles are the primary substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers; family Bible records; gravestone inscriptions; town meeting books that incidentally record vital events.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist churches were established in many Vermont towns as settlement began (1760s–1780s). Baptist and Methodist congregations formed in the 1780s. Quaker meetings existed in some communities.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (christenings), marriages, burials, membership lists, and in some congregations, confession-of-faith records. Confirmations were not a standard feature of Congregationalist or Baptist practice, so they are not a separate dated event series here.
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Where held:** Records of surviving congregations may be at the local church, at denominational archives (Congregationalist records often at the Congregational Library in Boston; Baptist records with the American Baptist Historical Society), or microfilmed by FamilySearch. The FamilySearch topic-specific Vermont Church Records page did not return Vermont-specific content at the time of this survey — consult FamilySearch.org directly.
- **Access:** Varies. Some have been transcribed by the Vermont Historical Society or county genealogical societies. Physical-only for many.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal decennial census was taken in 1790. Vermont appears in the 1790 census (taken after its March 1791 admission) — this is the earliest national enumeration for Vermont. It lists heads of household by name with counts of free white males, females, and other persons; it does not name individuals other than heads of household.
- **Pre-statehood enumerations:** No Vermont-specific census was conducted during the Republic of Vermont period. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Vermont Census did not return Vermont-specific content at the time of this survey.
- **Tax lists as census substitutes:** Vermont towns conducted tax assessments; these lists name property-holding residents and are critical substitutes for missing census coverage before 1790.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census for Vermont is indexed and available with images on Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). Tax lists are primarily physical or microfilm.

### Probate and court records
- **Structure:** The Republic of Vermont established probate courts organized at the county level. Vermont's original counties (Bennington, Windham, Windsor, Chittenden, Addison, Orange, Caledonia, Essex) were created between 1778 and 1792.
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianships, estate inventories. These begin with county formation dates — the earliest Vermont probate records date from 1778 (Bennington County).
- **Where held:** Vermont county probate courts still hold their own records; the Vermont State Archives has some collections. FamilySearch has microfilmed Vermont probate records.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Check the relevant county probate index for both will books (testate) and administration files (intestate). For the pre-statehood period, intestate administration records are especially valuable because they name heirs.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Probate Records page** did not return Vermont-specific content at the time of this survey — consult FamilySearch.org directly.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds, following New England practice. Vermont is a state-land state — the federal rectangular survey system does not apply.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Three overlapping grant authorities created the complexity of this period:
  1. New Hampshire Governor Benning Wentworth issued township grants ("New Hampshire Grants") from 1749 through 1764. These records are held by the New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Management.
  2. New York issued competing patents from 1764 onward. These records are at the New York State Archives in Albany.
  3. The Republic of Vermont's own land office confirmed and re-granted lands from 1777 onward. Vermont State Archives holds these.
- **The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** This record, noted specifically in the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy), was prepared under New York colonial authority and enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. It predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.
- **Town proprietors' records:** Individual towns maintained proprietors' records documenting original land divisions. These are held at town offices or Vermont State Archives and are among the most genealogically rich sources for this period.
- **Types:** Township grants, individual deeds, land patents, mortgages, tax records.
- **Where held:** Town land records (deeds) at town clerk offices; state-level grants at Vermont State Archives and New Hampshire/New York archives as described.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Land and Property page** did not return Vermont-specific content at the time of this survey.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (ended 1763, predates most Vermont settlement); Revolutionary War 1775–1783 (central to this period); Shays' Rebellion (Massachusetts, 1786–1787, minor Vermont involvement).
- **Green Mountain Boys:** Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys were organized before statehood and served throughout the Revolution. Vermont also raised its own Continental Line regiments.
- **Record types:**
  - Revolutionary War service records and pension files: held at NARA (National Archives), many digitized and indexed on Fold3.com (subscription) and Ancestry.com.
  - Bounty land warrants: NARA and Vermont State Archives.
  - Vermont state militia records: Vermont State Archives.
  - Pension files are especially genealogically valuable — they often contain depositions naming spouses, children, marriage dates, and witnesses.
- **Access:** NARA Fold3 (subscription), Ancestry.com (subscription), FamilySearch (free, partial).

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Vermont has many early burial grounds, including town cemeteries, family plots, and church cemeteries established as settlement began in the 1760s–1780s.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com, free) has significant Vermont coverage. BillionGraves also indexes some Vermont stones.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they exist are at town offices. The Vermont Old Cemetery Association has surveyed and published records from many historic cemeteries.
- **Value:** For the pre-statehood period, gravestones may be the only surviving record of a birth or death date. Inscriptions sometimes include age at death, allowing a birth year calculation, and occasionally name parents or spouse.

### Newspaper records
- **Early Vermont newspapers:** Vermont's first newspaper was the Vermont Gazette, founded in Westminster in 1781. The Vermont Journal (Windsor) began in 1783. Coverage for the 1760–1780 period is essentially nonexistent; newspapers become a viable source from the early 1780s onward.
- **Where held:** The Vermont Historical Society and Vermont State Library hold collections. Newspapers.com (subscription) and Chronicling America (free, Library of Congress) have some digitized Vermont newspapers, though coverage for this early period is thin.
- **Content value:** Death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices (estate sales, land sales, sheriff's notices), and town news. For the 1780s, newspapers are worth checking despite sparse coverage.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Vermont in the pre-statehood period was a destination, not a port of entry. Settlers arrived overland from southern New England — primarily Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Hampshire — not by sea.
- **No ocean passenger arrivals apply** to the vast majority of Vermont settlers in this period; the families had been in New England for generations.
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable for this period — settlers were native-born British colonists who became U.S. citizens at independence.
- **Emigration from Vermont:** Some families left Vermont after the Revolution for New York or later for Ohio and other territories. If your ancestor disappears from Vermont records after 1791, check western New York land records and Ohio territorial records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town-level property tax lists ("grand lists") and poll taxes. These were conducted annually and are the primary substitute for missing census coverage before 1790.
- **Date range:** Town grand lists begin with each town's establishment. Some survive from the early 1780s.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices and Vermont State Archives. FamilySearch has microfilmed some.
- **Substitute value:** Grand lists name all taxable male inhabitants and their property. For any year before 1790, these are the most reliable way to place an ancestor in a specific Vermont town.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records and proprietors' records:** Town meeting minutes record appointments, disputes, road grants, and poor relief, and often name residents not captured in any other source. Proprietors' records document original land division among founding settlers. These are at town offices and Vermont State Archives, and are essential for the 1760–1791 period.
- **Court records:** The Republic of Vermont established its own court system. County court records (civil suits, criminal cases) begin with county formation (1778 onward for the earliest counties). Vermont State Archives holds these.
- **Published town histories:** The FamilySearch Wiki specifically notes that "Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860-1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) These are a high-priority source. Many are available on Google Books, Hathi Trust, and the Internet Archive.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | 1790 federal census; microfilmed probate, land, and vital records (coverage varies by town); the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 federal census (indexed + images); Revolutionary War pension files (Fold3 partnership); some Vermont vital records and newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA originals) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records, headstone transcriptions and photos | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Some early Vermont newspapers from the 1780s onward | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (loc.gov/collections/chronicling-america) | Free digitized historic newspapers; Vermont coverage for this period is sparse | Free |
| Hathi Trust / Google Books / Internet Archive | Published Vermont town histories (1860–1900), many in the public domain | Free |
| New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Management | New Hampshire land grants (Wentworth grants) for Vermont territory | Contact for access |
| New York State Archives | New York patents issued over the Grants territory | Contact for access |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `external_links_search` tool returned 6 results for Vermont in this time window, all generic national-level links (U.S. Federal Census — Ancestry, Vital Records Wiki, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA). No Vermont-specific curated external collections were returned. The FamilySearch `collections_search` and `volume_search` tools were not invoked separately (the wiki was the primary tool); consult FamilySearch.org directly for the current list of Vermont digitized collections.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (Montpelier) | Republic of Vermont records, state land office grants, early court records, military records, some town records | In-person or written request; some finding aids online |
| Vermont Historical Society (Barre) | Manuscripts, town histories, genealogical collections, newspaper holdings, cemetery surveys | In-person; some materials online |
| Town clerk offices (each Vermont town) | Town meeting records, proprietors' records, grand lists (tax), early vital records, deeds | In-person or mail |
| County probate courts | Wills, administrations, guardianships from county formation dates (1778+) | In-person or mail |
| New Hampshire Division of Archives (Concord, NH) | Benning Wentworth's New Hampshire land grants for Vermont territory | In-person or written request |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York colonial patents for the Grants territory | In-person or online finding aids |
| National Archives (NARA, Washington DC / regional) | 1790 federal census, Revolutionary War service records, pension files | In-person; many online via Fold3/Ancestry |
| Congregational Library (Boston, MA) | Congregationalist church records from New England including early Vermont | In-person or written request |
| American Baptist Historical Society | Baptist church records | Contact for access |

## Records NOT online
- Town clerk grand lists (tax lists) before 1790 — primarily physical or microfilm
- Town meeting and proprietors' records — primarily physical at town offices or Vermont State Archives
- Most early church registers (Congregationalist, Baptist) — physical at local churches or denominational archives
- County court records (civil and criminal) from 1778–1791 — physical at Vermont State Archives
- New Hampshire land grants (Wentworth patents) — physical at New Hampshire Division of Archives; some transcriptions in published town histories
- New York colonial patents for Vermont territory — physical at New York State Archives
- Early probate records (1778–1791) — physical at county probate courts; some microfilmed

## Known record losses
- No catastrophic statewide courthouse fire is documented for Vermont as of this survey, but individual town office losses have occurred. The uneven survival of town clerk records noted by the FamilySearch Wiki ("survive unevenly") reflects loss as well as non-creation.
- Because Vermont had no established colonial government, there is no equivalent of a colonial church establishment that would have created comprehensive registers. The absence of records in this period is often a feature of the frontier settlement context, not loss.
- The period 1760–1777 (before the Republic of Vermont was organized) is the most poorly documented — the territory was effectively ungoverned at the civil level during much of this time.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.** The FamilySearch Wiki identifies this as the earliest systematic resident list for Vermont, enumerating approximately 1,800 grantees. If your ancestor held land in the Grants area before statehood, they may appear here. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **The 1790 federal census is your baseline.** It is the first national enumeration in which Vermont residents appear. Work backward from 1790 using tax lists and land records.
- **Search at the town level, not the county level.** Vermont's recording system is town-based. Knowing your ancestor's town is essential before searching vital records, deeds, or town meeting books.
- **Read the published town history.** The FamilySearch Wiki specifically flags that 19th-century town histories "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) Many are free on Hathi Trust and the Internet Archive. This is one of the first steps for pre-statehood research.
- **Check all three land-grant series.** A family that settled before 1777 may appear in New Hampshire grants (held in Concord, NH), New York patents (held in Albany, NY), and Vermont Republic re-grants (held in Montpelier, VT). These are three separate archives — not one.
- **Revolutionary War pension files are rich genealogical sources.** They frequently contain depositions naming spouses, children, marriage dates, and co-signers. Many Vermont veterans filed pensions. Search Fold3.com and Ancestry.com.
- **Cross the borders.** Vermont borders New Hampshire across the Connecticut River (Cheshire and Grafton counties on the NH side) and New York across Lake Champlain and the Taconic range (Albany, Washington, and Clinton counties on the NY side). Families near these borders generated records on both sides. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Neighboring Counties table for Vermont at the time of this survey, but the cross-border instruction stands.
- **Congregationalist church records are a vital substitute.** In the absence of civil vital registration, Congregationalist baptism, marriage, and burial entries from the 1770s and 1780s are the closest equivalent. Locate the church your ancestor's town family attended, then contact both the local church and the Congregational Library in Boston.
- **Town grand lists (tax records) replace missing census years.** For any year before 1790, annual grand lists are usually the best way to establish that an ancestor was in a specific Vermont town in a specific year.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki topic-specific pages** (Vermont Vital Records, Vermont Land and Property, Vermont Church Records, Vermont Probate Records, Vermont Census, Vermont Naming Customs) did not return Vermont-specific content during this survey. Check them directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/ for the most current guidance.
